title: Abraham Maslow: Needs-Hierarchy Theory
overview: Abraham Maslow, the founder of humanistic psychology, rejected theories built on disturbed patients and instead studied the healthiest, most fulfilled people to discover the full range of human potential. He proposed a hierarchy of five instinctoid needs (physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem and self-actualization) in which stronger, lower deficit needs generally take precedence over weaker, higher growth needs, plus cognitive needs to know and understand. Self-actualizers, 1 percent or less of people, are driven by metamotivation toward metaneeds and share traits such as efficient perception of reality, acceptance, creativeness and peak experiences; most people fail to self-actualize because the need is weak, childhood conditions are poor or they fear their own potential (the Jonah complex). The chapter covers Maslow's life, his optimistic image of human nature, assessment with the POI, research on needs, belongingness, self-esteem and self-determination theory, and criticisms of his methods alongside his broad influence.
objectives: Explain the humanistic criticisms of psychoanalysis and behaviourism and Maslow's approach of studying the healthiest people.
Relate Maslow's life, including his childhood and turn from behaviourism, to his theory.
Describe the five-level hierarchy of needs and the characteristics of needs, including deficit versus growth needs.
Explain the conditions for and exceptions to self-actualization and the role of cognitive needs.
Distinguish metamotivation from D-motivation and define metaneeds and metapathology.
List and explain the characteristics of self-actualizers, including peak experiences.
Explain why few people self-actualize, including child-rearing factors and the Jonah complex.
Describe Maslow's image of human nature and his assessment methods, including the POI and Smartphone Basic Needs Scale.
Summarise research on the hierarchy, belongingness, self-esteem, self-actualization, peak experiences and self-determination theory.
Critically evaluate Maslow's theory and its influence.

sections.heading: Maslow and the Humanistic Approach
sections.detailed:
Abraham Maslow is presented as the founder and spiritual leader of the humanistic psychology movement. His theory grew out of a rejection of the two dominant forces in psychology at the time: behaviourism and psychoanalysis, especially Freud's version of personality theory.

The criticism of psychoanalysis. Maslow argued that when psychologists build their picture of human nature mainly from abnormal or emotionally disturbed people, they end up ignoring everything that is positive in human beings, such as happiness, contentment and peace of mind. A psychology built only on the sick, he felt, underestimates what people can become. Behaviourism, for its part, struck him as having little to do with real people and their inner lives (a point his life story makes clear, since he moved from behaviourism to humanism).

Studying the best, not the average. Maslow's alternative was to study the most creative, healthy and mature people he could find, society's outstanding representatives. He used an analogy from athletics: if you want to know how fast human beings can run, you do not study the average runner but the fastest runner available. Only by studying the best examples can we see the full range of human potential.

The basis of the theory. For this reason his theory does not come from case histories of clinical patients (as Freud's did) but from research on creative, independent, self-sufficient and fulfilled adults. From this work he concluded that every person is born with the same set of instinctive needs, and that these needs make it possible for us to grow, develop and fulfil our potential. This optimistic, growth-centred view runs through the rest of the chapter: the hierarchy of needs, self-actualization, metamotivation and his image of human nature.

Exam angle. A question asking what humanistic psychologists objected to in behaviourism and psychoanalysis should stress (1) the narrow focus on abnormal and disturbed people, (2) the neglect of positive qualities and human potential, and (3) Maslow's remedy of studying the healthiest, most fully developed people.
sections.simple: Maslow started humanistic psychology because he felt Freud and the behaviourists only looked at the sick or at mechanical behaviour. He wanted to study the healthiest, most creative people to see how far humans can go. His theory says we are all born with needs that push us to grow.
keyPoints: Maslow is regarded as the founder and spiritual leader of humanistic psychology.
He objected to both behaviourism and psychoanalysis, particularly Freud.
Studying only disturbed people ignores positive qualities like happiness, contentment and peace of mind.
Fastest-runner analogy: to know human potential, study the best people, not the average.
His theory came from research on healthy, creative, self-sufficient adults, not clinical case histories.
Everyone is born with the same instinctive needs that enable growth and fulfilment.

sections.heading: The Life of Maslow (1908-1970)
sections.detailed:
Maslow's life is told under several sub-headings, and the chapter uses it to show how his personal history fed into his theory.

A miserable childhood. Maslow was born in 1908 in Brooklyn, New York, the eldest of seven children of poor, poorly educated immigrant parents. He later said it was a wonder he had not become psychotic given his childhood. His father was distant, drank, chased women and periodically abandoned the family; Maslow felt anger toward him as a boy but eventually reconciled with him. His relationship with his mother was far worse. She openly preferred his younger siblings, showed him no affection, punished him harshly for small misdeeds and warned that God would punish him. When he brought home two stray kittens she killed them in front of him. He never forgave her, refused to attend her funeral, and later said that his whole life-philosophy and research had its roots in his revulsion against everything she stood for.

Alone in the world. Maslow believed he was ugly because of his large nose and felt inferior because of his thin build; his parents mocked his appearance, his father once calling him the ugliest child anyone had seen at a family gathering. He described his adolescence as one big inferiority complex and a feeling of being all alone and somehow wrong. He tried to compensate by pushing himself toward athletic achievement. The chapter notes that the man who would later admire Alfred Adler was himself a living example of Adler's idea of compensation for inferiority feelings.

Finding a new style of life. When athletics failed to bring recognition, he turned to books. The library became his playground; he would wait on its steps before it opened and arrive at school early to read books his teacher lent him. These early memories, in Adlerian terms, point to the style of life he would build: a life of scholarship as the way out of poverty and loneliness. His grades were mediocre and he was on academic probation after his first year at City College of New York, but persistence improved them. He tried law at his father's request, dropped it after two weeks, and wanted instead to study "everything."

Becoming a behaviourist. He married his cousin Bertha when he was 20 and she was 19; marriage gave him belonging and direction, and he said his life had little meaning before it. He had found a psychology course at Cornell bloodless and unrelated to people, but at the University of Wisconsin he discovered John B. Watson's behaviourism and, like many in the early 1930s, believed it could solve the world's problems. His experimental training included research on dominance and sexual behaviour in primates.

From monkeys to self-actualization. The shift to humanism came from several influences: the onset of World War II and the birth of his first child, which made him feel small and not in control (he said anyone who had a baby could not be a behaviourist). He earned his Ph.D. at Wisconsin in 1934, held a postdoctoral fellowship under E. L. Thorndike at Columbia, and taught at Brooklyn College until 1951. He scored an IQ of 195 on tests, which Thorndike called genius level, and he liked to mention it in conversation. In New York he met emigre intellectuals including Karen Horney and Alfred Adler (Bertha recalled he talked about Adler constantly), as well as Max Wertheimer and Ruth Benedict, whose qualities later sparked his ideas about self-actualization.

A parade changes his life. In 1941, watching a parade shortly after the Pearl Harbor attack, he resolved to build a psychology of the highest human ideals, to improve human personality and to show that people can do better than prejudice, hatred and aggression.

Becoming famous. He taught at Brandeis University from 1951 to 1969, then moved to California on a foundation grant to work on a humanistic philosophy of politics, economics and ethics. He became hugely popular, won many honours, and was elected president of the American Psychological Association in 1967. Despite stomach problems, insomnia, depression and heart disease, he worked even harder, admitting in 1968 that he had given up plays, poetry and new friends for his work. He died in 1970 of a heart attack while jogging, as his cardiologist had advised.
sections.simple: Maslow had a lonely, poor and abusive childhood and felt ugly and inferior, which he tried to overcome through sport and then books. He began as a behaviourist studying monkeys, but fatherhood, World War II and meeting people like Wertheimer and Benedict turned him toward studying the best in humans. He became a famous psychologist and APA president before dying in 1970.
keyPoints: Born 1908 in Brooklyn, eldest of seven; hostile mother, aloof father, deep hatred of his mother shaped his life-philosophy.
Felt ugly and inferior; compensated through athletics and then scholarship, illustrating Adler's compensation and style of life.
Married cousin Bertha; trained as a behaviourist at Wisconsin under Watson's influence, studying primate dominance and sexuality.
Turned humanistic after his first child's birth, World War II and the 1941 parade after Pearl Harbor.
Influenced by Adler, Horney, Wertheimer and Benedict; IQ of 195 per Thorndike.
Taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis; APA president 1967; died of a heart attack in 1970.

sections.heading: Personality Development: The Hierarchy of Needs
sections.detailed:
The core of Maslow's theory is a hierarchy of five innate needs that activate and direct human behaviour. From bottom to top they are: physiological needs, safety needs, belongingness and love needs, esteem needs, and the need for self-actualization (Figure 9.1).

Instinctoid needs. Maslow called these needs instinctoid, meaning they have a hereditary component; we are born with them. However, the behaviours we use to satisfy them are learned, so the way the needs are met differs from one person to another. This is the basis of Maslow's view that personality reflects both heredity and environment.

Order of strength. The needs are ordered from strongest at the bottom to weakest at the top. A lower need must be at least partly satisfied before a higher one can influence behaviour. A hungry person, for example, has no urge to win esteem from others; all attention goes to getting food. Only when people have enough food and shelter and the other lower needs are met do higher needs become motivating.

One need dominates at a time. We are not driven by all the needs at once. Generally only one need dominates personality at any given moment, and which one depends on which others have already been satisfied. People who are successful in their careers, for instance, have their physiological and safety needs well looked after and are more likely to be driven by esteem or self-actualization.

The order can change. The hierarchy is not fixed for life. If a recession costs someone their job, safety and physiological needs can take priority again: paying the mortgage becomes more important than popularity with colleagues or a civic award. This shows that the dominant need depends on present circumstances, not only on stage of life.

Exam angle. When describing the hierarchy, list all five levels in order, define instinctoid, explain prepotency (lower before higher), mention that only one need dominates at a time, and give the recession example to show that the order can shift. Then add the characteristics of needs and the exceptions described in the following sections.
sections.simple: Maslow said we have five built-in needs stacked like a pyramid: body needs, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization. The lower ones are stronger and must be at least partly met before the higher ones matter. Usually one need runs the show at a time, and losing a job can drop you back down the pyramid.
keyPoints: Five innate needs: physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualization.
Instinctoid: the needs are hereditary, but the behaviours that satisfy them are learned and vary.
Arranged from strongest (bottom) to weakest (top); lower needs must be partly met first.
Usually only one need dominates personality at a time.
The order can change, e.g., job loss in a recession brings safety and physiological needs back to the fore.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Needs
sections.detailed:
Maslow described several general characteristics that apply to the needs in his hierarchy.

1. Strength and priority. The lower a need sits in the hierarchy, the greater its strength, potency and priority. Higher needs are weaker needs.

2. Higher needs appear later in life. Physiological and safety needs arise in infancy. Belongingness and esteem needs arise in adolescence. The need for self-actualization does not appear until midlife.

3. Deficit (deficiency) needs. Because higher needs are less necessary for survival, their satisfaction can be postponed, and failing to satisfy them does not cause a crisis. Failing to satisfy a lower need does produce a crisis. For this reason Maslow called the lower needs deficit or deficiency needs: not meeting them leaves a deficit or lack in the person.

4. Growth (being) needs. Although higher needs are less essential for staying alive, they contribute to personal growth. Satisfying them leads to better health, happiness, contentment, fulfilment and longer life. Maslow therefore called them growth or being needs; they involve realizing and fulfilling human potential.

5. External conditions. Satisfying higher needs requires better social, economic and political circumstances than satisfying lower needs. Pursuing self-actualization, for example, needs more freedom of expression and opportunity than pursuing safety.

6. Partial satisfaction. A need does not have to be completely satisfied before the next one becomes important. Maslow proposed a declining percentage of satisfaction as one moves up the hierarchy. In his hypothetical example, a person might satisfy 85 percent of physiological needs, 70 percent of safety needs, 50 percent of belongingness and love needs, 40 percent of esteem needs, and 10 percent of the self-actualization need.

Deficit versus growth needs (for comparison questions). Deficit needs are lower, stronger, appear early, are essential for survival, produce a crisis when unmet and can be satisfied in poorer conditions. Growth needs are higher, weaker, appear later, are less essential for survival, can be postponed without crisis, require more favourable conditions, and when satisfied enhance health, happiness and longevity. Maslow's own interest lay mainly in the growth needs and self-actualization, which is why his research focused on self-actualizers.

Do we always satisfy needs in a fixed order? Generally yes, because lower needs are prepotent. But the chapter qualifies this: needs only need to be partly met, the order can be reversed by circumstances such as job loss, and some people satisfy higher needs while frustrating lower ones (see Achieving Self-Actualization in Non-Traditional Ways).
sections.simple: Lower needs are stronger and show up first in life; higher needs are weaker and appear later, with self-actualization only in midlife. Unmet lower needs cause a crisis, so Maslow called them deficit needs; higher needs help us grow, so he called them growth or being needs. You do not need to fully satisfy one level before the next kicks in.
keyPoints: Lower needs are stronger and have priority; higher needs are weaker.
Physiological and safety needs appear in infancy, belongingness and esteem in adolescence, self-actualization in midlife.
Deficit (deficiency) needs: unmet lower needs produce a crisis and a lack.
Growth (being) needs: higher needs aid health, happiness, fulfilment and longevity.
Higher needs require better social, economic and political conditions.
Declining percentage of satisfaction: 85, 70, 50, 40 and 10 percent in Maslow's example.

sections.heading: Physiological Needs
sections.detailed:
Physiological needs are the most basic and powerful needs in the hierarchy: needs for food, water, air, sleep and sex (the chapter summary lists these; Figure 9.1 shows food, water and sex).

Their power when unmet. The chapter illustrates their strength with experiences most people can recognise: struggling for air underwater, or going too long without food. In such moments, love, esteem or anything else feels trivial. A starving person craves only food.

A satisfied need no longer motivates. Once a physiological need is met, it stops driving behaviour. It ceases to direct or control what the person does. This is a key principle in Maslow's system: a gratified need no longer serves as a motivator.

Culture and affluence. For most people in affluent, industrialized cultures, physiological needs are rarely a concern; middle-class Americans seldom worry about basic survival. As a result these needs play only a minimal role in motivating most people in such societies. They have much greater personal impact in cultures where everyday survival remains a struggle. (A photo caption in the chapter makes the same point: when food and shelter are lacking, esteem and self-actualization become much less important.)

Exam angle. Stress (1) prepotency of physiological needs, (2) the principle that satisfied needs no longer motivate, and (3) the influence of economic conditions and culture on how important these needs are.
sections.simple: Physiological needs are the body's basics like food, water, air and sleep. When you are starving or out of breath, nothing else matters. But once they are met they stop motivating you, which is why they matter little for most people in rich societies.
keyPoints: The strongest needs: food, water, air, sleep and sex.
When unmet, they override all other needs; a starving person craves only food.
Once satisfied, a need no longer directs or controls behaviour.
In affluent, industrialized cultures they play a minimal motivating role.
They are far more influential where daily survival is a concern.

sections.heading: Safety Needs
sections.detailed:
Safety needs are needs for security, stability, order and freedom from fear and anxiety.

Infants and children. Maslow saw safety needs as important drives mainly for infants and neurotic adults. In children they are easy to observe because youngsters react visibly and immediately to any threat to their security, whereas adults have learned to inhibit such reactions. Children also show their safety needs through a preference for structure and routine, for an orderly and predictable world. Too much freedom and permissiveness removes structure and order and is likely to make children anxious and insecure. Children should be given some freedom, but only within the limits of their ability to cope, and with guidance, because they cannot yet direct their own behaviour or foresee its consequences.

Neurotic adults. Neurotic and insecure adults also need structure and order because their safety needs still dominate their personality. They compulsively avoid new experiences and arrange their world to be predictable, budgeting time and organising possessions; the chapter's example is keeping pencils in perfectly neat rows and hanging all shirts facing the same way.

Normal adults. Emotionally healthy adults have usually satisfied their safety needs, but these needs can still influence them. Many people prefer the predictable to the unknown and order to chaos, which is why we save for the future, buy insurance and stay in a secure job rather than risk a new venture. Still, safety needs are not nearly as overwhelming for normal adults as for children or neurotics.

Safety versus belongingness (comparison). Safety needs concern security, order, predictability and freedom from fear, are dominant in infancy and in neurotics, and are met through stable structure and routine. Belongingness and love needs emerge after physiological and safety needs are reasonably satisfied, concern giving and receiving love and being accepted by others, and are met through close relationships and group membership.
sections.simple: Safety needs are about feeling secure, having order and not being afraid. Kids show them clearly and need routine, with limited, guided freedom. Neurotic adults stay stuck here and over-organise their lives, while normal adults show it mildly through things like saving and buying insurance.
keyPoints: Needs for security, stability, order and freedom from fear and anxiety.
Most important for infants and neurotic adults.
Children prefer routine; too much permissiveness causes anxiety; freedom should be limited and guided.
Neurotics compulsively avoid novelty and make their world rigidly predictable.
Normal adults show safety needs mildly, e.g., saving, insurance, secure jobs.

sections.heading: Belongingness and Love Needs
sections.detailed:
Once physiological and safety needs are reasonably well satisfied, people turn to the needs for belongingness and love.

How they are satisfied. These needs can be met through a close relationship with a friend, lover or mate, or through social relationships within a group. The chapter adds that they can also be developed and maintained through social media, which allows people to keep in touch with others at any moment and from anywhere. The chapter summary adds that they can be satisfied through affectionate relations with one person or with people in general.

Giving and receiving love. The need involves both giving and receiving love, and it can be satisfied in an intimate relationship with another person.

Love is not sex. Maslow did not equate love with sex. Sex belongs among the physiological needs, though he accepted that sex is one way of expressing the love need.

Consequence of failure. Maslow suggested that failing to satisfy the need for love is a fundamental cause of emotional maladjustment.

Link to research. Later in the chapter, research shows how powerful the belongingness need is: some psychologists consider it as strong as the needs for food and water, and studies of ostracism show that thwarting it affects memory, self-esteem and feelings of control (see Research: The Belongingness Need).
sections.simple: After basic and safety needs, we want to belong and to give and get love, through friends, partners, groups, or even social media. Maslow said love is not the same as sex. Not getting love is a major cause of emotional problems.
keyPoints: Emerge once physiological and safety needs are reasonably met.
Satisfied through friends, lovers or mates, groups, and even social media.
Involves both giving and receiving love.
Love is not sex: sex is physiological, though it can express love.
Failure to satisfy love needs is a fundamental cause of emotional maladjustment.

sections.heading: Esteem Needs
sections.detailed:
Once people feel loved and have a sense of belonging, they may be driven by the need for esteem, which takes two forms.

1. Esteem from oneself (self-esteem): feelings of self-worth and respect for oneself.

2. Esteem from others: status, recognition and social success, that is, respect given by other people.

Effects of satisfaction. Satisfying the need for self-esteem lets us feel confident of our strength, worth and adequacy. This helps us become more competent and productive in all areas of life.

Effects of frustration. When self-esteem is lacking, we feel inferior, helpless and discouraged, with little confidence in our ability to cope.

Link to Adler and to research. The description of the frustrated esteem need echoes the inferiority feelings Maslow himself experienced as a child. Later in the chapter, a large body of research on self-esteem supports Maslow's claim that people high in self-esteem feel more worthy, confident, competent and productive, and that low self-esteem is linked with anxiety, depression and many other problems.

Note on order. Although esteem normally comes after belongingness, the chapter notes a common reversal: some people value esteem more than love, believing they can only be loved once they feel self-confident.
sections.simple: Esteem needs come in two flavours: respecting yourself, and getting respect, status and recognition from others. Meeting them makes you confident and productive. Missing them makes you feel inferior, helpless and discouraged.
keyPoints: Two forms: self-esteem (self-worth) and esteem from others (status, recognition, social success).
Emerge after belongingness and love needs are met.
Satisfaction brings confidence in one's strength, worth and adequacy, and greater competence and productivity.
Frustration brings feelings of inferiority, helplessness and discouragement.
Some people reverse the order, putting esteem before love.

sections.heading: The Self-Actualization Need
sections.detailed:
Self-actualization is the highest need in the hierarchy. It means the maximum realization and fulfilment of one's potentials, talents and abilities; the glossary defines it simply as the fullest development of the self.

Restlessness without it. Even a person who has satisfied every other need will feel restless, frustrated and discontented if he or she is not self-actualizing. Maslow expressed this by saying that a musician must make music, an artist must paint and a poet must write in order to be at peace.

Open to everyone. The process can take many forms. Maslow believed that anyone, whatever their occupation or interests, can maximise their abilities and reach the fullest personality development. Self-actualization is not reserved for creative or intellectual stars such as musicians, artists and writers. What matters is fulfilling one's own potential, whatever it is, at the highest possible level. In one of his memorable remarks, Maslow said a first-rate soup is more creative than a second-rate painting, and that cooking, parenting or homemaking can be creative while poetry need not be.

Place in the hierarchy. As the highest need, self-actualization is also the weakest and appears last, not until midlife. It needs favourable conditions and can easily be blocked, which explains why few people achieve it (see Failure to Become Self-Actualizing). The next sections describe the conditions required for it and the ways some people pursue it out of the usual order.
sections.simple: Self-actualization is becoming the best version of yourself, fully using your talents. Even if everything else in life is fine, you will feel restless if you are not doing this. It is not just for artists or geniuses; a great cook or parent can be self-actualizing too.
keyPoints: Highest need: maximum realization of one's potentials, talents and abilities (fullest development of the self).
Without it a person feels restless, frustrated and discontented even if other needs are met.
'A musician must make music' to be at peace.
Open to anyone in any occupation; not limited to creative superstars.
A first-rate soup can be more creative than a second-rate painting.

sections.heading: Conditions for Achieving Self-Actualization
sections.detailed:
Maslow listed several conditions that must be in place before a person can satisfy the need for self-actualization.

1. Freedom from constraints. We must be free of restrictions imposed both by society and by ourselves.

2. Freedom from distraction by lower needs. We must not be preoccupied with physiological, safety, belongingness or esteem needs. This follows from the principle that lower needs must be at least partly met before higher ones can operate.

3. Security in self-image and relationships. We must feel secure in our self-image and in our relationships with others, and be able both to love and to be loved in return.

4. Realistic self-knowledge. We must have a realistic understanding of our strengths and weaknesses, our virtues and our vices.

Connecting the conditions to the rest of the theory. The first condition links to the characteristic of needs that higher needs require better external social, economic and political circumstances, such as freedom of expression and opportunity. The second and third reflect the prepotency of lower needs, especially love and esteem. The fourth anticipates two characteristics of self-actualizers: efficient perception of reality and acceptance of self, others and nature. The chapter summary repeats that self-actualization requires a realistic knowledge of one's strengths and weaknesses.
sections.simple: To self-actualize you need to be free from limits set by society or yourself, not be stuck worrying about basic needs, feel secure and loved, and know your real strengths and weaknesses.
keyPoints: Freedom from constraints imposed by society and by oneself.
Not being distracted by lower-order needs.
Security in self-image and relationships; ability to love and be loved.
Realistic knowledge of one's strengths and weaknesses, virtues and vices.

sections.heading: Achieving Self-Actualization in Non-Traditional Ways
sections.detailed:
Although the hierarchy applies to most people, Maslow recognised exceptions in which the usual order is reversed.

Sacrifice for an ideal. Some people dedicate their lives to an ideal and willingly give up everything for their cause. People have fasted until death for their beliefs, denying their physiological and safety needs.

Religious renunciation. Religious figures may give up all worldly goods to keep a vow of poverty, satisfying the self-actualization need while frustrating lower needs.

Artists. Throughout history, artists have risked their health and security for the sake of their work.

Esteem before love. A more common reversal occurs when people value esteem more than love, believing they can satisfy their belongingness and love needs only after they first feel self-confident.

Significance. These exceptions show that the hierarchy describes a general tendency, not a rigid law. Together with the points that needs only need partial satisfaction and that circumstances like a recession can change priorities, they help answer the review question about whether we always satisfy needs in a fixed order: usually, but not always.
sections.simple: Not everyone follows the pyramid in order. Some people starve for a cause, give up all possessions for religion, or risk their health for art, putting self-actualization above basic needs. A more everyday flip is when people chase esteem before love.
keyPoints: The hierarchy has exceptions; it is a general tendency, not a fixed rule.
People may fast to death for beliefs, denying physiological and safety needs.
Religious figures may take vows of poverty, satisfying self-actualization while frustrating lower needs.
Artists have risked health and security for their work.
Common reversal: placing esteem above love, believing love comes only after self-confidence.

sections.heading: Cognitive Needs
sections.detailed:
Later in his career Maslow proposed a second set of innate needs, the cognitive needs: the need to know and the need to understand. These exist outside the five-level hierarchy. The need to know is stronger than the need to understand, so it must be at least partly satisfied before the need to understand can emerge.

Evidence for the cognitive needs (Maslow, 1970b):
- Laboratory studies show animals exploring and manipulating their surroundings for no apparent reason other than curiosity, a desire to know and understand.
- History shows people seeking knowledge even at the risk of their lives, placing the needs to know and understand above safety needs.
- Studies suggest that emotionally healthy adults are attracted to mysterious and unexplained events and are motivated to learn more about them.
- In his own clinical practice, Maslow saw emotionally healthy adults who complained of boredom and lack of zest; he called them intelligent people leading stupid lives in stupid jobs. They improved when they took up more challenging activities that satisfied the needs to know and understand.

How the cognitive needs affect personality. The needs to know and understand appear in late infancy and early childhood and show up as natural curiosity. Because they are innate they need not be taught, but parents and teachers can inhibit a child's spontaneous curiosity. Failure to satisfy them is harmful and hampers the full development and functioning of personality.

Relation to the main hierarchy. This two-need hierarchy overlaps the five-need hierarchy. Knowing and understanding, essentially finding meaning in our environment, are basic to dealing with the world in an emotionally healthy, mature way in order to satisfy all five needs. It is impossible to become self-actualizing without meeting the needs to know and understand.

Exam angle (review question). We develop the needs to know and understand in late infancy and early childhood; the need to know is the stronger of the two.
sections.simple: Maslow later added two more inborn needs: to know and to understand. Knowing comes first because it is stronger. They show up as curiosity in early childhood, and you cannot self-actualize without them.
keyPoints: Cognitive needs: the need to know and the need to understand, outside the five-need hierarchy.
The need to know is stronger and must be partly met before the need to understand emerges.
Evidence: animal curiosity, people risking life for knowledge, attraction to mysteries, bored patients who improved with challenge.
Appear in late infancy and early childhood as natural curiosity; can be inhibited by parents and teachers.
They overlap the main hierarchy; self-actualization is impossible without them.

sections.heading: The Study of Self-Actualizers: Metamotivation
sections.detailed:
According to Maslow, self-actualizers differ from other people in their basic motivation. He proposed a special kind of motivation for them called metamotivation (also called B-motivation, for Being). The prefix meta means after or beyond, so metamotivation goes beyond psychology's traditional idea of motivation.

D-motivation. Maslow described the motivation of people who are not self-actualizing as D-motivation (Deficiency). It means striving for something specific to make up for something that is lacking. For example, not eating produces a bodily deficiency felt as discomfort, which motivates action to reduce the tension: a specific need (hunger) requires a specific goal object (food) and produces action to get it. Maslow's writing on this is incomplete, but D-motivation seems to apply not only to physiological needs but also to safety, belongingness and love, and esteem needs.

Metamotivation: fulfilling potential. In contrast, self-actualizers are concerned with fulfilling their potential and with knowing and understanding their environment. In a state of metamotivation they are not trying to reduce tension, satisfy a deficiency or reach a specific object. Instead they aim to enrich their lives by increasing tension, seeking a variety of stimulating and challenging experiences. Because their lower deficiency needs have been met, they operate beyond striving for goal objects. They are in a state of "being," expressing their full humanity spontaneously, naturally and joyfully. In this sense self-actualizers are said to be developing from within rather than striving toward goals.

Metaneeds. Since self-actualizers are in a sense unmotivated in the usual way, Maslow proposed a list of metaneeds toward which they evolve (Table 9.1). Metaneeds are states of being, such as goodness, uniqueness and perfection, rather than specific goal objects. Table 9.1 lists: truth, goodness, beauty, unity or wholeness, dichotomy-transcendence, aliveness or process, uniqueness, perfection, necessity, completion or finality, justice, order, simplicity, richness or totality or comprehensiveness, effortlessness, playfulness, self-sufficiency, and meaningfulness.

Metapathology. Failure to satisfy metaneeds is harmful and produces metapathology, which thwarts full development of personality. It prevents self-actualizers from expressing, using and fulfilling their potential. They may feel helpless and depressed without being able to identify the source of the feelings or a goal that would relieve them (the summary calls it a formless illness with no specific identifiable cause). Each metaneed has its own metapathology, for example: truth / mistrust, cynicism, scepticism; goodness / hatred, disgust, reliance only on self; beauty / vulgarity, restlessness, loss of taste; unity / disintegration; dichotomy-transcendence / black-and-white, either-or thinking; aliveness / deadness, robotizing, loss of zest; uniqueness / loss of individuality, feeling anonymous; perfection / hopelessness; necessity / chaos; completion / incompleteness, cessation of striving; justice / anger, lawlessness, total selfishness; order / insecurity, wariness; simplicity / over-complexity, confusion; richness / depression, loss of interest in the world; effortlessness / fatigue, strain, clumsiness; playfulness / grimness, humourlessness; self-sufficiency / responsibility given to others; meaningfulness / meaninglessness, despair.

D-motivation versus B-motivation (summary for comparison). D-motivation: reduces tension, makes up a lack, aims at a specific goal object, applies to the four lower needs. B-motivation: increases tension, enriches life, has no specific goal object, aims at metaneeds as states of being, applies to self-actualizers.
sections.simple: Ordinary people are driven by what they lack (D-motivation), like eating to fix hunger. Self-actualizers have their basic needs covered, so they are driven to grow and seek challenge (metamotivation or B-motivation), aiming at states like truth, beauty and goodness called metaneeds. If metaneeds are blocked, they get a vague sick, depressed feeling called metapathology.
keyPoints: Metamotivation (B-motivation): growth from within, increasing tension, not aimed at a specific goal object.
D-motivation: striving to make up a deficiency and reduce tension; applies to the four lower needs.
Metaneeds are states of being such as truth, goodness, beauty, uniqueness and perfection (Table 9.1).
Metapathology: thwarted self-development from unmet metaneeds; helplessness and depression without a clear cause.
Each metaneed has a matching metapathology, e.g., truth / mistrust and cynicism; meaningfulness / despair.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Self-Actualizers
sections.detailed:
Maslow's research on emotionally healthy people formed the basis of his personality theory. He found few self-actualizers, estimating that they make up 1 percent or less of the population, but concluded that they share certain characteristics (Table 9.2).

1. Efficient perception of reality. They see the world and other people clearly and objectively, without prejudgments or preconceptions.

2. Acceptance of themselves, others and nature. They accept their own strengths and weaknesses, do not distort their self-image and do not feel guilty about failings. They also accept the weaknesses of others and of society.

3. Spontaneity, simplicity and naturalness. Their behaviour is open, direct and natural. They rarely hide their feelings or play a role to please society, though they may do so to avoid hurting others. They are individualistic in ideas and ideals but not necessarily unconventional in behaviour, and secure enough to be themselves without being overly assertive.

4. Focus on problems outside themselves. They have a sense of mission or commitment to which they devote their energy. This dedication to a cause or vocation is a requirement for self-actualization. They find pleasure in hard work; through it they satisfy the metaneeds, and it challenges their abilities and helps define their sense of self.

5. Detachment and need for privacy. They can experience isolation without harm and seem to need solitude more than others. They depend on themselves for satisfaction, which can make them look aloof, though that is not their intent; they are simply more autonomous and do not crave social support.

6. Freshness of appreciation. They experience the world with freshness, wonder and awe, enjoying repeated experiences (a sunset, a painting, a symphony, a baseball game, a gift) as if for the first time, and take little for granted.

7. Mystical or peak experiences. They know moments of intense ecstasy, similar to deep religious experiences, which can occur in almost any activity. During these peak experiences the self is transcended and the person feels supremely powerful, confident and decisive.

8. Social interest. Borrowing Adler's concept, Maslow described their sympathy and empathy for all humanity. Though often irritated by others' behaviour, they feel kinship and understanding and want to help.

9. Profound interpersonal relations. Their circle of friends is small, but their friendships are deep and lasting, usually with people of similar qualities. They often attract admirers or disciples, but these relationships tend to be one-sided, with the admirer asking more than the self-actualizer can or will give.

10. Creativeness. They are highly creative, inventive and original in work and life. They are flexible, spontaneous and willing to make and learn from mistakes, open and humble like children before society teaches them embarrassment.

11. Resistance to enculturation. They are autonomous, independent and self-sufficient, free to resist social and cultural pressures. They do not openly rebel against norms but are governed by their own nature rather than society's strictures.

Table 9.2 also lists tolerance and acceptance of others, and the chapter summary adds a democratic character structure.

Human flaws. Self-actualizers seem nearly perfect, but they are not. They can occasionally be rude or even ruthless, and they experience doubts, conflicts and tension; however, these incidents are rarer and less intense than in people who are not self-actualizing.

Are peak experiences necessary? Peak experiences are listed among the shared characteristics of self-actualizers, and the chapter says self-actualizers know such moments; but it also says they can occur with virtually any activity. The chapter does not state outright that they are a strict requirement; the one characteristic it explicitly calls a requirement is dedication to a cause or vocation.
sections.simple: Maslow said self-actualizers (1 percent or fewer of people) see reality clearly, accept themselves and others, act naturally, are devoted to a mission, like privacy, appreciate everyday things freshly, have peak experiences, care for humanity, have a few deep friendships, are creative, and resist social pressure. They are not perfect and can sometimes be rude or ruthless.
keyPoints: Self-actualizers are 1 percent or less of the population.
Efficient perception of reality; acceptance of self, others and nature; spontaneity, simplicity and naturalness.
Focus on problems outside themselves (dedication to a cause is a requirement); detachment and need for privacy.
Freshness of appreciation; mystical or peak experiences in which the self is transcended.
Social interest (from Adler); profound but few relationships; creativeness; resistance to enculturation.
They still have flaws: occasional rudeness, ruthlessness, doubts and conflicts, but less often and less intensely.

sections.heading: Failure to Become Self-Actualizing
sections.detailed:
If self-actualization is innate and does not have to be learned, why do fewer than 1 percent of people achieve it? The chapter gives several reasons.

1. It is the weakest need. The higher a need in the hierarchy, the weaker it is, and self-actualization, as the highest, is the weakest of all. It is easily inhibited. Hostile or rejecting parents, for example, make it hard to satisfy love and esteem needs, so the self-actualization need may never emerge. At a lower level, poor economic conditions make it hard to satisfy physiological and safety needs, so self-actualization becomes less important.

2. The importance of childhood. Inadequate education and improper child-rearing can block the drive for self-actualization in adulthood.
- Sex-role training: Maslow cited the typical training of boys to suppress tenderness and sentimentality, so that part of their nature does not develop fully.
- Overprotection: children who are not allowed to try new behaviours, explore ideas or practise new skills are likely to become inhibited adults, unable to express themselves fully in activities vital to self-actualization.
- Excessive permissiveness: too much freedom in childhood can cause anxiety and insecurity, undermining safety needs.
- The ideal is a balance of permissiveness and regulation.
- Sufficient love in childhood is a prerequisite for self-actualization, as is satisfying physiological and safety needs in the first two years of life. Children who feel secure and confident early remain so as adults. This resembles Erikson's emphasis on developing trust in early childhood and Horney's idea of the childhood need for security. Without enough parental love, security and esteem, adult self-actualization is difficult.

3. The Jonah complex. Named after the biblical Jonah, who was called by God to prophesy, feared the task, tried to run away, found nowhere to hide and finally accepted his fate. The Jonah complex refers to doubts about our own abilities: the fear that maximising our potential will lead to situations we cannot cope with. We are both afraid of and thrilled by the possibilities, but too often the fear wins.

4. It takes courage. Self-actualization requires courage. Even with the lower needs met, fulfilment does not simply happen; it takes effort, discipline and self-control. For many people it seems easier and safer to accept life as it is than to seek new challenges. Self-actualizers constantly test themselves by abandoning secure routines and familiar behaviours and attitudes.

Exam angle. For "Why do so few people self-actualize?" cover weakness of the need, environmental and economic barriers, childhood factors (sex roles, overprotection, permissiveness, lack of love), the Jonah complex and the need for courage. For "What child-rearing practices thwart self-actualization?" focus on sex-role training, overprotection, excessive permissiveness and insufficient love and security.
sections.simple: Few people self-actualize because it is the weakest need and is easily blocked by poor conditions or cold parents. Overprotective, over-permissive or unloving parenting, and teaching boys not to be tender, also hold people back. Some people fear their own potential (the Jonah complex), and growth simply takes courage.
keyPoints: Self-actualization is the weakest need and easily inhibited by rejecting parents or poor economic conditions.
Childhood matters: sex-role training, overprotection and excessive permissiveness can thwart it; balance is ideal.
Enough love and security in the first years is a prerequisite (similar to Erikson's trust and Horney's security).
Jonah complex: fear that maximizing our potential will bring situations we cannot cope with.
Self-actualization takes courage, effort, discipline and self-control; it means leaving secure routines.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Maslow's view of personality is humanistic and optimistic. He focused on health rather than illness, growth rather than stagnation, and virtues and potentials rather than weaknesses and limitations. He had strong confidence in our ability to shape our lives and our society.

Free will versus determinism. We have free will to choose how best to satisfy our needs and realise our potential. We can create an actualizing self or refrain from doing so. We are therefore ultimately responsible for the level of personality development we reach or fail to reach.

Nature versus nurture. The needs in Maslow's hierarchies are innate, but the behaviours that satisfy them are learned. So personality is determined by the interaction of heredity and environment, of personal and situational variables.

Uniqueness versus universality. Though not explicit in his writings, Maslow seemed to favour uniqueness. Motivations and needs are universal, but the ways they are satisfied vary because they are learned. Even self-actualizers, who share qualities, do not behave identically.

Role of childhood. Maslow accepted that early childhood experiences can foster or inhibit adult development, but he did not believe we are victims of them. We have more potential than we realise to manage our lives and society and would be happier and more productive if we learned to do so.

Ultimate goal. Self-actualization as the ultimate and necessary goal reflects his belief that, given the right conditions, we can reach the highest level of human functioning.

Good versus evil. Maslow believed human nature is basically good, decent and kind, but he did not deny evil. He wrote privately that some people were evil beyond reclamation. He saw wickedness not as inherited but as the result of an inappropriate environment.

Contrast with Freud (review question). The chapter says Maslow objected to Freud's approach because it was built on abnormal and disturbed people and so ignored positive human qualities. Maslow's own image, drawn from healthy people, stresses health over illness, free will and conscious choice, uniqueness, the ability to overcome childhood experiences rather than being their victim, innate goodness, and growth toward self-actualization; it is openly optimistic. For the Freud side of a full comparison, students should draw on the earlier Freud chapter of the book.
sections.simple: Maslow was an optimist: he saw people as basically good, free to choose, responsible for their own growth, and shaped by both genes and environment. Childhood matters but does not trap us. Evil, he thought, comes from a bad environment, not from nature.
keyPoints: Optimistic and humanistic: focus on health, growth and potential.
Free will: we choose how to satisfy needs and are responsible for our development.
Needs are innate but satisfying behaviours are learned: heredity and environment interact.
Favours uniqueness; childhood matters but we are not its victims.
Human nature is basically good; evil results from an inappropriate environment.
Ultimate goal is self-actualization.

sections.heading: Assessment in Maslow's Theory
sections.detailed:
Maslow's work on self-actualization did not start as a formal programme of personality assessment. It began with curiosity about two people he greatly admired: the anthropologist Ruth Benedict and the Gestalt psychologist Max Wertheimer. He wanted to understand what made them so different from other people, and after careful observation concluded that they shared certain qualities that set them apart from the average person.

Searching for self-actualizers. He then tried to assess these qualities in other people. His first subjects were college students, but he found only 1 in 3,000 whom he could call self-actualizing. He concluded that the qualities he saw in Benedict and Wertheimer were not yet developed in young people. He turned next to middle-aged and older people, but even among them fewer than 1 percent met his criteria.

His final sample. The self-actualizers he finally identified numbered several dozen, classified as certain or highly probable cases, partial cases, or potential cases. Some were his contemporaries; others were historical figures, including Thomas Jefferson, Albert Einstein, George Washington Carver (an African-American scientist of the early 20th century), Harriet Tubman (a former slave who became an abolitionist before the Civil War) and Eleanor Roosevelt (the president's wife and a prominent social activist).

Techniques. For historical figures he analysed biographical material and written records for shared personal characteristics. For living subjects he used interviews, free association and projective tests. Many living subjects became self-conscious when questioned, so he often had to study them indirectly, though he never explained exactly how.

Later measures. Two self-report measures are described next: Shostrom's Personal Orientation Inventory and the Smartphone Basic Needs Scale.
sections.simple: Maslow started by studying two people he admired, Ruth Benedict and Max Wertheimer. He found almost no self-actualizers among students (1 in 3,000) and fewer than 1 percent among older adults. He studied living people with interviews, free association and projective tests, and historical figures like Einstein and Eleanor Roosevelt through biographies.
keyPoints: Began informally from admiration for Ruth Benedict and Max Wertheimer.
Only 1 of 3,000 college students qualified; fewer than 1 percent of middle-aged and older people.
Final sample: several dozen certain, partial or potential cases, including Jefferson, Einstein, Carver, Tubman and Eleanor Roosevelt.
Historical figures: biographical analysis; living subjects: interviews, free association, projective tests.
Self-conscious subjects were often studied indirectly, method unexplained.

sections.heading: The Personal Orientation Inventory
sections.detailed:
The Personal Orientation Inventory (POI) is a self-report questionnaire developed by psychologist Everett Shostrom (1964, 1974) to measure self-actualization.

Format. It consists of 150 pairs of statements. For each pair, respondents choose the statement that applies more to them. Sample items (Table 9.3) contrast, for example, doing what others expect versus feeling free not to; needing to justify one's actions or feelings versus not needing to; always living by society's rules versus not always needing to; expressing only warm feelings to friends versus expressing both warm and hostile feelings; growing by aiming at a socially approved goal versus growing best by being oneself; and always controlling anger versus expressing honestly felt anger. In each pair, the second, more autonomous choice reflects self-actualization.

Scoring. The POI is scored for 2 major scales and 10 subscales. The two major scales are:
- Time competence: the degree to which a person lives in the present.
- Inner directedness: the degree to which a person depends on himself or herself rather than on others for judgments and values.

Research use. Later in the chapter, POI scores are shown to correlate positively with emotional health, creativity, well-being after therapy, academic achievement, autonomy and racial tolerance, and negatively with alcoholism, institutionalization, neuroticism, depression and hypochondriasis. POI research on women aged 19 to 55 supported the idea that self-actualization develops gradually over the life span.
sections.simple: The POI is Shostrom's test of self-actualization: 150 pairs of statements where you pick the one that fits you. It gives two main scores: time competence (living in the present) and inner directedness (relying on yourself, not others).
keyPoints: Developed by Everett Shostrom (1964, 1974) to measure self-actualization.
Self-report: 150 pairs of statements; choose the more applicable one.
Scored for 2 major scales and 10 subscales.
Time competence: living in the present.
Inner directedness: relying on oneself rather than others for judgments and values.

sections.heading: The Smartphone Basic Needs Scale
sections.detailed:
The Smartphone Basic Needs Scale is a 20-item self-report inventory designed to assess how far smartphone use can satisfy the needs in Maslow's system.

Development. It was developed with college students in the United States and South Korea as subjects, and its developers (Kang & Jung, 2014) reported high validity and reliability.

Sample items. To measure the belongingness need, respondents chose any statements that applied to them, completing the stem "By using my smartphone, I can..." with items such as getting closer to important people around them, meeting nice people, developing relationships, getting along with people well, and working and communicating together.

Significance. The scale reflects the chapter's point that belongingness needs can now be met partly through social media and technology, and shows how Maslow's hierarchy is still being applied to new areas of life.
sections.simple: This 20-item test checks how much using a smartphone meets Maslow's needs. Kang and Jung built it with US and South Korean students and found it valid and reliable. For example, belongingness items ask whether your phone helps you get closer to people or make friends.
keyPoints: 20-item self-report inventory of how smartphone use satisfies Maslow's needs.
Developed with US and South Korean college students (Kang & Jung, 2014).
Reported high validity and reliability.
Belongingness items include getting closer to important people and developing relationships.

sections.heading: Research on Maslow's Theory: Methods and the Hierarchy of Needs
sections.detailed:
Maslow's methods. Maslow did not use case studies, experiments or correlational methods. Critics charged that his study of self-actualizers was neither rigorous nor controlled, and Maslow agreed, admitting that by ordinary laboratory standards it was not research at all. He argued that self-actualization could not be studied by accepted scientific procedures, so the alternatives were to wait for suitable techniques or not study it at all. Too impatient and too committed to helping humanity to wait, he said careful experiments would take too long given the years he had left. He called his work pilot studies, expected others to confirm it, and believed that because his conclusions were correct he needed less data than other theorists.

Research on the hierarchy of needs.
- Williams and Page (1989): among male and female college students, satisfaction of safety, belongingness and esteem needs was negatively related to neuroticism and depression. Esteem needs were stronger than belongingness needs, and safety needs were of little concern, as expected for people who can afford college.
- Lester (1990): using the Need Satisfaction Inventory, a self-report measure of how well Maslow's needs are satisfied, college students' scores were correlated with the Eysenck Personality Inventory; higher need satisfaction went with lower neuroticism.
- Graham and Balloun (1973): with a sample representative of the general population, the order of the five needs was supported. Concern about each need increased from lowest to highest: physiological needs, presumably well met, were of little concern, while self-actualization was of greatest interest because it is hardest to satisfy.
- Noltemeyer, Bush, Patton and Bergen (2012): economically disadvantaged youth in the Midwestern United States focused mainly on satisfying safety needs and showed little concern for higher needs, consistent with Maslow.
- Tay and Diener (2011): a study of more than 40,000 people in 123 countries supported the view that physiological and safety needs must be satisfied before people can achieve fulfilment and happiness.
- Taormina and Gao (2013); Ivtzan, Gardner, Bernard, Sekhon and Hart (2013): the more basic needs are satisfied, the greater the chance that higher needs are also satisfied; people older than 36 are far more likely to achieve self-actualization than younger people (consistent with self-actualization emerging in midlife).
sections.simple: Maslow admitted his research was not scientific by lab standards; he called it pilot studies and expected others to confirm it. Later studies largely support the hierarchy: need satisfaction goes with less neuroticism, the order of needs holds, poor youth focus on safety, a 123-country study found basic needs come first, and people over 36 are likelier to self-actualize.
keyPoints: Maslow did not use case studies, experiments or correlations and admitted his work was not rigorous research.
He called it pilot studies and believed he needed less data because he was right.
Williams & Page (1989) and Lester (1990): need satisfaction linked to lower neuroticism (and depression).
Graham & Balloun (1973) supported the order of needs; concern rose from lowest to highest need.
Noltemeyer et al. (2012): poor youth focused on safety; Tay & Diener (2011): basic needs first across 123 countries.
People older than 36 are more likely to self-actualize (Taormina & Gao; Ivtzan et al., 2013).

sections.heading: Research: The Belongingness Need
sections.detailed:
The belongingness need can be satisfied only through association with, and especially acceptance by, other people. Some psychologists consider it as powerful a drive as the physiological needs for food and water.

Gardner, Pickett and Brewer (2000). American college students who believed they were in an Internet chat room were excluded and ignored: no one responded to their messages while others chatted happily. Afterwards they read a diary supposedly written by a student and recalled as many activities from it as they could. Students whose need to belong had been thwarted recalled significantly more social events than students whose need to belong had been satisfied. The researchers concluded that failure to satisfy the need to belong can influence cognition, such as memory, and the kinds of events a person recalls.

Smith and Williams (2004). College students led to believe they had been excluded or rejected in an Internet chat room reported lower self-esteem, control and belongingness than students who had not been told they were ostracized. These negative feelings developed within only 8 minutes of learning of their exclusion.

Collisson (2013); Seehusen et al. (2013). People in the Netherlands and the United States who were high in the need to belong assumed others were also high in it, and the need to belong triggered nostalgia for a past in which, in memory at least, they had felt a greater sense of belonging.

Begen and Turner-Cobb (2012). American teenagers who felt a sense of belonging were physically healthier than those who did not.

Conclusion. Satisfying the need to belong has important consequences for behaviour, thought and feelings, supporting Maslow's emphasis on belongingness and love.
sections.simple: Research shows that being left out hurts quickly: people excluded in fake chat rooms remembered more social events and felt lower self-esteem within 8 minutes. People with high belonging needs feel nostalgic, and teens who feel they belong are healthier.
keyPoints: Belongingness requires acceptance by others; some see it as powerful as hunger and thirst.
Gardner, Pickett & Brewer (2000): excluded students recalled more social events, so thwarted belonging affects memory.
Smith & Williams (2004): online ostracism lowered self-esteem, control and belonging within 8 minutes.
Collisson; Seehusen et al. (2013): high need to belong projects onto others and triggers nostalgia.
Begen & Turner-Cobb (2012): teens who feel they belong are physically healthier.

sections.heading: Research: Self-Esteem (High and Low Self-Esteem)
sections.detailed:
Many studies have examined Maslow's need for self-esteem, a characteristic everyone has to some degree.

High self-esteem. Research supports Maslow's view that people high in self-esteem have greater self-worth and self-confidence, feel more competent and productive, and function better in many situations.
- Ellis and Taylor (1983): college students with high self-esteem received more job offers and were rated more favourably by recruiters.
- Shamir (1986): people with high self-esteem coped better with job loss.
- Campbell, Rudich and Sedikides (2002): high self-esteem people saw themselves as significantly higher in intellectual skills, agreeableness and morality, and as more extraverted.
- Bowker (2006); Pyszczynski et al. (2004): young adults in the US and Canada with high self-esteem were more likely to play school sports and had less anxiety and defensive behaviour.
- Noser and Zeigler-Hill (2014): women college students with unstable self-esteem (shifting between high and low) had a much stronger desire to become famous than those with stable self-esteem.

Low self-esteem.
- Large-scale programmes in the United States, Iceland, Canada, China, Norway and New Zealand (Brown, 2010; Cai, Wu & Brown, 2009; Donnellan et al., 2005; Jonsdottir et al., 2008; Moksnes et al., 2010; Trzesniewski et al., 2006) linked low self-esteem to anxiety, depression, smoking, school dropout, criminal convictions, financial problems, strong emotional reactions to negative outcomes and difficulties at work.
- Routledge et al. (2010); Stinson et al. (2008): in Canada and China, low self-esteem was linked to more physical health problems and more anxiety about death.
- Crocker and Luhtanen (2003): low self-esteem students had significantly more social adjustment problems.
- Seidah and Bouffard (2007): over one-third of Canadian adolescents in grades 7, 9 and 11 said their perceived attractiveness determined their self-esteem; those more concerned with appearance had lower self-esteem; no sex differences.
- Nezlek, Kowalski, Leary, Blevins and Holgate (1997): people low in self-esteem who believed they were deliberately excluded from a lab group felt significantly more rejected than high self-esteem people.
- Crocker and Park (2004): failing to reach self-esteem goals, such as high grades or job success, increased anger, shame, sadness and worthlessness.
- Swann, Chang-Schneider and McClarty (2007): low self-esteem people may think and act in self-defeating ways that diminish their quality of life.
- Kalpidou, Costin and Morris (2011); Mehdizadeh (2010); Vogel et al. (2014): students with lower self-esteem spent more time on Facebook and other social networking sites.
- Bushman, Moeller and Crocker (2011); Salamon (2011): students valued self-esteem boosts such as praise or high grades more than favourite food, alcohol, time with a friend, a paycheck or sex.

These findings are summarised in the chapter's Highlights box: high self-esteem goes with competence, job offers, coping, emotional health and strong ethnic identity; low self-esteem with depression, dropout, criminal convictions, social and health problems, lower quality of life and more time on social media.
sections.simple: High self-esteem people get more job offers, cope better with job loss, rate themselves as smarter and nicer, and are less anxious. Low self-esteem is linked worldwide with depression, anxiety, smoking, dropping out, crime, health problems and more time on Facebook. Students even value self-esteem boosts over food or sex.
keyPoints: High self-esteem: more job offers (Ellis & Taylor), better coping with job loss (Shamir), more positive self-views (Campbell et al.).
Unstable self-esteem linked with a strong desire for fame (Noser & Zeigler-Hill, 2014).
Low self-esteem linked across six countries with anxiety, depression, smoking, dropout, crime, money and work problems.
Low self-esteem: more health problems and death anxiety, social adjustment problems, stronger feelings of rejection.
Appearance concern predicts lower teen self-esteem (Seidah & Bouffard, 2007).
Lower self-esteem students spend more time on Facebook; students prize self-esteem boosts over food, money or sex.

sections.heading: Research: Self-Esteem and Other Behaviours, Stability over Time, Ethnic and Cultural Differences
sections.detailed:
Effects of self-esteem on other behaviours.
- Van Hiel and Brebels (2011): in Belgium and the United States, among older people (average age 71), conservative political beliefs were related to high self-esteem; with age people became more conservative and felt better about themselves.
- Ziegler-Hill and Myers (2009): in the 2008 US presidential primaries and election, people were much more likely to vote for candidates they believed had higher self-esteem.

Stability of self-esteem over time.
- Gentile, Twenge and Campbell (2010); Orth and Robins (2014); Orth, Trzesniewski and Robins (2010): self-esteem increases during adolescence and adulthood, peaks at about age 60, then declines.
- Huang (2010b): in Taiwan, self-esteem increased through childhood, adolescence and early adulthood but changed very little after age 30.
- Wagner, Lang, Neyer and Wagner (2014): in Germany, being married (usually post-adolescent) and high subjective well-being were linked to high self-esteem.
(Note: the chapter summary describes self-esteem as high in childhood, low in adolescence, rising in adulthood and falling in middle and old age; the main text describes a rise through adolescence and adulthood to a peak near 60.)

Ethnic and cultural differences.
- Shaw, Liang and Krause (2010): Black teenagers report higher self-esteem than White teenagers; Black self-esteem rises through adulthood but declines more steeply after 60.
- Eaton, Livingston and McAdoo (2010): Black women college students who identified strongly with Black culture had much higher self-esteem.
- Peteet, Brown, Lige and Lanaway (2014): Black college students who felt incompetent despite contrary evidence scored high in stress and low in self-esteem.
- Schmitt and Allik (2005); Tafarodi et al. (2011); Yamaguchi et al. (2007): across more than 50 countries, Japanese college students consistently scored lowest in self-esteem.
- Fong and Mashek (2014): Asian-American students generally reported lower self-esteem than European Americans, but those with stronger social connections in their dorms scored higher.
- Caldwell et al. (2006); Swenson and Prelow (2005): high self-esteem correlated with delinquency among Mexican-American teenage boys.
- Kim, Hogge and Salvisberg (2014): first-generation Mexican immigrants who felt most pressure to adopt American practices had lower self-esteem.
- Verkuyten (2009): in the Netherlands, Turkish and Moroccan immigrants who identified more strongly with their ethnic background had higher self-esteem.
- Lopez (2008): among US immigrants from Puerto Rico, stronger ethnic identity went with higher self-esteem.

Pattern. Strong ethnic identity and social connection tend to raise self-esteem, while pressure to assimilate lowers it; Japanese students score lowest cross-nationally.
sections.simple: Self-esteem even affects politics: older people with high self-esteem are more conservative, and voters favour candidates who seem confident. Self-esteem generally rises until about 60 and then falls. Strong ethnic identity tends to raise self-esteem, pressure to assimilate lowers it, and Japanese students score lowest across 50+ countries.
keyPoints: High self-esteem linked to conservatism in older people and to voting for confident-seeming candidates.
Self-esteem rises through adolescence and adulthood, peaks around 60, then declines (in Taiwan, little change after 30).
Marriage and subjective well-being linked to high self-esteem in Germany.
Black teens report higher self-esteem than White teens; strong Black cultural identity raises it.
Japanese students score lowest across 50+ countries; Asian Americans lower than European Americans.
Strong ethnic identity raises self-esteem; pressure to assimilate lowers it; high self-esteem linked to delinquency in one sample.

sections.heading: Research: Self-Actualization and Peak Experiences
sections.detailed:
Self-actualization. Higher self-actualization scores on the POI have been positively related to emotional health, creativity, well-being after therapy, academic achievement, autonomy and racial tolerance. Other studies show negative correlations between high self-actualization scores and alcoholism, institutionalization for mental disturbance, neuroticism, depression and hypochondriasis. These results are in the directions expected from Maslow's description of self-actualizers. POI research on women aged 19 to 55 confirmed Maslow's view that self-actualization develops gradually across the life span.

Peak experiences. Research on Americans aged 40 to 65 (Hoffman, Kaneshiro & Compton, 2012) found that the three most commonly reported peak experiences involved joyful experiences with other people, a sense of achievement, and personal growth.

Cross-cultural comparisons (Ho, Chen & Hoffman, 2012; Ho, Chen, Hoffman, Guan & Iversen, 2013):
- Mainland Chinese reported more peak experiences involving serenity.
- Chinese residents of Hong Kong reported more involving interpersonal joy and external achievement.
- People in Brazil and Portugal most often reported peak experiences tied to developmental landmarks such as finishing college, marrying or getting a first job.

Exam angle. For the review question on what correlational research reveals about self-actualization and personality, list the positive and negative correlates of POI scores and note that they fit Maslow's description.
sections.simple: People who score high on the POI tend to be emotionally healthy, creative, autonomous and tolerant, and are less likely to be depressed, neurotic or alcoholic. Peak experiences usually involve joy with others, achievement or growth, and their content differs across cultures.
keyPoints: POI scores correlate positively with emotional health, creativity, post-therapy well-being, academic achievement, autonomy and racial tolerance.
POI scores correlate negatively with alcoholism, institutionalization, neuroticism, depression and hypochondriasis.
Women aged 19-55: self-actualization develops gradually over the life span.
Americans 40-65: peak experiences involve joy with others, achievement and personal growth (Hoffman et al., 2012).
Mainland Chinese: serenity; Hong Kong: interpersonal joy and achievement; Brazil and Portugal: developmental landmarks.

sections.heading: Self-Determination Theory
sections.detailed:
Self-determination theory is described as a contemporary outgrowth of the essence of Maslow's self-actualization theory. It proposes that people have an innate tendency to express their interests, to exercise and develop their capabilities and potentials, and to overcome challenges (Deci & Ryan, 2009, 2012; Ryan & Deci, 2000).

Supporting research. Evidence has come from diverse groups, such as football players in Australia, teenagers in India and Nigeria, and older women in the United States. Those who scored highest in self-determination showed the greatest improvement in overall behaviour and subjective well-being (Deci, 2011; Podlog & Eklund, 2010; Sheldon, Abad & Omoile, 2009; Stephan, Boiche & LeScanff, 2010).

More recent research in the United States, Belgium, China, Peru, Australia, Mexico, Venezuela, the Philippines, Malaysia and Japan has further supported the role of self-determination in facilitating positive growth needs and self-actualization (Chen et al., 2014; Church et al., 2013).

The Highlights box adds that people high in self-determination tend to have satisfied the needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness, to be high in self-esteem and self-actualization, and to possess an innate tendency to overcome challenges and develop their capabilities.

Link to Maslow. Like Maslow's self-actualization need, self-determination is an innate tendency toward growth and fulfilment of potential. The three basic needs it proposes are discussed in the next section.
sections.simple: Self-determination theory, by Deci and Ryan, is a modern version of Maslow's idea: we are born wanting to use and grow our abilities and beat challenges. Studies across many countries show that people high in self-determination have better well-being.
keyPoints: A contemporary outgrowth of Maslow's self-actualization theory (Deci & Ryan).
Innate tendency to express interests, develop capabilities and overcome challenges.
Supported in Australian footballers, Indian and Nigerian teens, and older US women.
Highest self-determination scorers showed the most improvement in behaviour and well-being.
Further support across many countries for its role in growth needs and self-actualization.

sections.heading: Intrinsic Motivation
sections.detailed:
Intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation. Self-determination is facilitated by intrinsic motivation: doing an activity solely because of the interest and challenge of the activity itself. Extrinsic motivation, by contrast, means doing something only for an external reward such as praise, promotion, a pay rise or a higher grade.

Similarity to Maslow. There is a basic similarity between intrinsic motivation and self-determination on the one hand and Maslow's self-actualization on the other: both are concerned with fulfilling one's talents and abilities for inner satisfaction rather than external reward. (This parallels Maslow's contrast between metamotivation and D-motivation.)

Three basic needs. Self-determination theory proposes three basic needs whose satisfaction leads to well-being:
1. Competence: the need to feel that one can master difficult tasks.
2. Autonomy: the freedom to base one's actions on one's own interests, needs and values.
3. Relatedness: the need to feel closely connected with other people.

Supporting research. Satisfaction of these needs, among both young and elderly people in cultures as different as the United States, France and Russia, was positively associated with high self-esteem, self-actualization and psychological well-being (Ferrand, Martinent & Dumaz, 2014; Milyavskaya & Koestner, 2011; Ryan & Deci, 2000; Strizhitskaya & Davedyuk, 2014).

Comparison with Maslow's hierarchy. Relatedness resembles the belongingness and love need, competence resembles esteem, and autonomy resembles the independence and resistance to enculturation of self-actualizers.
sections.simple: Intrinsic motivation means doing something because you enjoy the challenge, not for rewards like money or grades. Self-determination theory says we need competence, autonomy and relatedness, and meeting them is linked to high self-esteem and well-being across cultures.
keyPoints: Intrinsic motivation: doing an activity for its own interest and challenge; extrinsic: for external rewards.
Both intrinsic motivation and self-actualization aim at inner satisfaction rather than external reward.
Three basic needs: competence, autonomy, relatedness.
Satisfying them is linked to self-esteem, self-actualization and well-being in the US, France and Russia, young and old.

sections.heading: Reflections on Maslow's Theory
sections.detailed:
Criticisms.
- Research methods and data: critics focus on his methods and the lack of experimentally generated support. His sample of self-actualizers, fewer than half of whom were interviewed in person, is too small to generalise to the population.
