- Vague and inconsistent procedures: he did not describe how he interpreted test results or analysed biographies, nor what led him to classify particular people as self-actualizing. (The chapter notes that weak methodology is not unique to Maslow.)
- Subjective selection: he chose people he admired, using personal criteria that were not specified at the time; he later admitted self-actualization was hard to describe accurately. His list of characteristics came solely from his clinical interpretations and may reflect his personal philosophy and moral values, so the descriptions may really portray Maslow's own ideal of a worthy, healthy person.
- Vague concepts: his definitions of metaneeds, metapathology, peak experiences and self-actualization could be inconsistent and ambiguous.
- Is self-actualization innate? Critics ask why it could not be learned, the product of some unique combination of childhood experiences.

Maslow's defence. He argued that although his theory lacked strong laboratory support, it succeeded in social, clinical and personal terms: it fitted most people's personal experience and gave them a structured theory that helped them make better sense of their inner lives.

Contributions and influence. Partly because of his optimism and compassion, his theory and humanistic psychology in general became extremely popular in the 1960s and 1970s. A formal school took shape: journals and organisations were founded and a division of humanistic psychology was formed within the American Psychological Association. Humanistic concerns were reborn in the positive psychology movement (discussed in Chapter 14), whose leaders credit humanistic psychology as a forerunner; the summary notes positive psychology focuses on subjective well-being. Maslow's legacy continues to influence personality, social psychology, developmental psychology and organisational behaviour (Kenrick, Griskevicius, Neuberg & Schaller, 2010). Few theories have had such broad impact beyond psychology: teachers, counsellors, business and government leaders, health care professionals and ordinary people have found his ideas useful in solving problems.

Exam angle. For a critical evaluation, balance the methodological criticisms (small, subjective sample; unspecified criteria; vague concepts; innateness questioned) against his defence and his wide influence, including the research support for the hierarchy, self-esteem and self-determination.
sections.simple: Critics say Maslow's research was unscientific: a tiny, hand-picked sample of people he admired, unclear criteria, and fuzzy concepts, so his self-actualizer might just be his personal ideal. Maslow replied that the theory works for people in real life. It became hugely popular, shaped humanistic and positive psychology, and is used in education, business and health care.
keyPoints: Criticised for small sample (fewer than half interviewed in person) and lack of experimental data.
Procedures vague; selection criteria unspecified; subjects were people he admired, so traits may reflect his own ideals.
Concepts like metaneeds, metapathology, peak experiences and self-actualization are ambiguous; innateness questioned.
Maslow's defence: the theory works in social, clinical and personal terms.
Hugely popular in the 1960s-70s; an APA division of humanistic psychology was formed; forerunner of positive psychology.
Broad influence on personality, social, developmental and organisational psychology and applied fields.

terms.definition: The movement Maslow founded and led, opposing behaviourism and psychoanalysis and focusing on positive human qualities, health and the full range of human potential.
Adler's idea, illustrated by young Maslow, of trying to overcome felt weaknesses (for him, appearance and build) by forcing development in another area such as athletics.
Maslow's arrangement of inborn needs from strongest to weakest (physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualization) that activates and directs behaviour.
Maslow's term for the innate needs in his hierarchy; they have a hereditary component, though the behaviours that satisfy them are learned.
The lower needs; failing to satisfy them produces a deficiency or lack and a crisis for the person.
The higher needs; less necessary for survival than deficit needs, they involve realizing and fulfilling human potential and improve health, happiness and longevity.
Maslow's proposal that each successive need is satisfied to a lesser degree, e.g., 85, 70, 50, 40 and 10 percent from physiological to self-actualization.
The most basic needs (food, water, air, sleep, sex); when unmet they dominate, but once met they no longer motivate.
Needs for security, stability, order and freedom from fear and anxiety; most important for infants and neurotic adults.
Needs to give and receive love and to be accepted, met through close relationships, groups and even social media.
Needs for esteem from oneself (self-worth) and from others (status, recognition, social success).
The fullest development of the self; the maximum realization of one's potentials, talents and abilities.
Innate needs to know and to understand, existing outside the five-need hierarchy; the need to know is stronger.
The motivation of self-actualizers, which involves maximizing personal potential rather than striving for a particular goal object; also called B-motivation.
Another name for metamotivation: growth-oriented motivation that increases tension and enriches life.
The motivation of non-self-actualizers: striving for a specific goal object to make up a lack and reduce tension; applies to the four lower needs.
States of growth or being (e.g., truth, goodness, beauty, uniqueness, perfection) toward which self-actualizers evolve.
A thwarting of self-development related to failure to satisfy the metaneeds; felt as helplessness and depression without an identifiable cause.
A metaneed in Table 9.1; its frustration produces black-and-white, either-or thinking and a simplistic view of life.
A moment of intense ecstasy, similar to a religious or mystical experience, during which the self is transcended and the person feels powerful, confident and decisive.
Adler's concept, adopted by Maslow, for the sympathy, empathy and kinship self-actualizers feel for all humanity.
The self-actualizer's freedom to resist social and cultural pressures, being governed by their own nature rather than society's strictures, without open rebellion.
The fear that maximizing our potential will lead to a situation with which we will be unable to cope; doubts about our own abilities.
Shostrom's self-report test of self-actualization made up of 150 pairs of statements, scored for 2 major scales and 10 subscales.
A major POI scale measuring the degree to which a person lives in the present.
A major POI scale measuring how much a person relies on himself or herself rather than others for judgments and values.
A 20-item self-report inventory (Kang & Jung, 2014) assessing how far smartphone use satisfies the needs in Maslow's system.
A self-report questionnaire measuring how well a person satisfies Maslow's needs, used by Lester (1990).
A contemporary outgrowth of Maslow's self-actualization theory (Deci & Ryan) proposing an innate tendency to express interests, develop capabilities and overcome challenges.
Engaging in an activity solely for the interest and challenge of the activity itself.
Engaging in an activity only for an external reward such as praise, promotion, pay or grades.
In self-determination theory, the need to feel that one can master difficult tasks.
In self-determination theory, the freedom to base one's actions on one's own interests, needs and values.
In self-determination theory, the need to feel a close connection with other people.
A later movement in which humanistic concerns were reborn; its leaders credit humanistic psychology as a forerunner.

people.name: Abraham Maslow
people.contribution: Founder and spiritual leader of humanistic psychology; proposed the needs hierarchy, cognitive needs, metamotivation and the study of self-actualizers.

people.name: Sigmund Freud
people.contribution: Maslow objected to Freud's approach for building a picture of human nature from abnormal and disturbed people.

people.name: Alfred Adler
people.contribution: Maslow's childhood exemplified Adler's compensation for inferiority; Maslow met Adler, was excited by his theories and adopted his concept of social interest.

people.name: E. Hoffman
people.contribution: Maslow's biographer (Hoffman, 1988, 1996), whose works are the source for many details of Maslow's hatred of his mother and his childhood.

people.name: Bertha Maslow
people.contribution: Maslow's cousin and wife; marriage gave him belonging and direction, and she recalled his excitement about Adler.

people.name: John B. Watson
people.contribution: Leader of behaviourism, whose ideas enraptured Maslow at Wisconsin before his turn to humanism.

people.name: E. L. Thorndike
people.contribution: Supervised Maslow's postdoctoral fellowship at Columbia and described his IQ of 195 as genius level.

people.name: Karen Horney
people.contribution: Emigre intellectual Maslow met in New York; her idea of the childhood need for security parallels Maslow's view of childhood.

people.name: Max Wertheimer
people.contribution: Gestalt psychologist whom Maslow admired; his outstanding qualities started Maslow's study of self-actualization.

people.name: Ruth Benedict
people.contribution: Anthropologist whom Maslow admired; with Wertheimer, she was the starting point of his research on self-actualizers.

people.name: Erik Erikson
people.contribution: His emphasis on early trust is likened to Maslow's view that love and security in childhood are prerequisites for self-actualization.

people.name: Albert Einstein, Thomas Jefferson, George Washington Carver, Harriet Tubman, Eleanor Roosevelt
people.contribution: Historical figures Maslow studied through biographical material as self-actualizers.

people.name: Everett Shostrom
people.contribution: Developed the Personal Orientation Inventory (1964, 1974) to measure self-actualization.

people.name: Kang and Jung
people.contribution: Developed the Smartphone Basic Needs Scale (2014) with US and South Korean students.

people.name: Deci and Ryan
people.contribution: Proposed self-determination theory, with its three basic needs of competence, autonomy and relatedness.

people.name: Kenrick, Griskevicius, Neuberg and Schaller
people.contribution: Cited (2010) for the continuing influence of Maslow's ideas on personality, social, developmental and organisational psychology.

studies.title: Maslow's search among college students
studies.finding: Only 1 of 3,000 college students could be called self-actualizing; even among middle-aged and older people fewer than 1 percent qualified.

studies.title: Williams & Page (1989): need satisfaction and adjustment
studies.finding: Among college students, satisfaction of safety, belongingness and esteem needs was negatively related to neuroticism and depression; esteem needs were stronger than belongingness, and safety needs of little concern.

studies.title: Lester (1990): Need Satisfaction Inventory
studies.finding: College students higher in need satisfaction scored lower in neuroticism on the Eysenck Personality Inventory.

studies.title: Graham & Balloun (1973): order of needs
studies.finding: In a representative sample the order of the five needs was supported, and concern rose from lowest (physiological) to highest (self-actualization) need.

studies.title: Noltemeyer, Bush, Patton & Bergen (2012): disadvantaged youth
studies.finding: Economically disadvantaged Midwestern US youth focused mainly on safety needs with little concern for higher needs.

studies.title: Tay & Diener (2011): 123 countries
studies.finding: In over 40,000 people across 123 countries, physiological and safety needs had to be satisfied before fulfilment and happiness.

studies.title: Taormina & Gao (2013); Ivtzan et al. (2013): basic needs and age
studies.finding: The more basic needs are satisfied, the more likely higher needs are; people over 36 are far more likely to self-actualize.

studies.title: Gardner, Pickett & Brewer (2000): chat-room exclusion and memory
studies.finding: Students excluded in a simulated chat room later recalled significantly more social events from a diary, showing thwarted belonging affects memory.

studies.title: Smith & Williams (2004): online ostracism
studies.finding: Students told they had been excluded online reported lower self-esteem, control and belongingness within only 8 minutes.

studies.title: Collisson (2013); Seehusen et al. (2013): need to belong
studies.finding: People high in the need to belong in the Netherlands and US assumed others were too, and the need triggered nostalgia for a more belonging past.

studies.title: Begen & Turner-Cobb (2012): belonging and health
studies.finding: American teenagers who felt they belonged were physically healthier.

studies.title: Ellis & Taylor (1983): self-esteem and job offers
studies.finding: College job applicants with high self-esteem received more job offers and were rated more favourably by recruiters.

studies.title: Shamir (1986): job loss
studies.finding: People high in self-esteem coped more effectively with job loss.

studies.title: Campbell, Rudich & Sedikides (2002): self-views
studies.finding: High self-esteem people rated themselves higher in intellectual skills, agreeableness, morality and extraversion.

studies.title: Bowker (2006); Pyszczynski et al. (2004): sports and anxiety
studies.finding: High self-esteem young adults in the US and Canada were more likely to play school sports and had lower anxiety and defensiveness.

studies.title: Noser & Zeigler-Hill (2014): unstable self-esteem and fame
studies.finding: Women college students with unstable self-esteem wanted fame much more strongly than those with stable self-esteem.

studies.title: Large-scale low self-esteem programmes (Brown, 2010; Donnellan et al., 2005; Trzesniewski et al., 2006 and others)
studies.finding: In six countries low self-esteem was linked to anxiety, depression, smoking, dropout, criminal convictions, financial problems, strong reactions to negative outcomes and work difficulties.

studies.title: Routledge et al. (2010); Stinson et al. (2008): health and death anxiety
studies.finding: In Canada and China low self-esteem was linked to more physical health problems and more anxiety about death.

studies.title: Crocker & Luhtanen (2003): social adjustment
studies.finding: College students low in self-esteem had significantly more social adjustment problems.

studies.title: Seidah & Bouffard (2007): appearance and self-esteem
studies.finding: Over one-third of Canadian adolescents said perceived attractiveness determined their self-esteem; greater appearance concern meant lower self-esteem; no sex differences.

studies.title: Nezlek, Kowalski, Leary, Blevins & Holgate (1997): rejection
studies.finding: Low self-esteem people who believed they were deliberately excluded from a group felt significantly more rejected than high self-esteem people.

studies.title: Crocker & Park (2004): failed self-esteem goals
studies.finding: Failing to reach self-esteem goals like high grades or job success increased anger, shame, sadness and worthlessness.

studies.title: Swann, Chang-Schneider & McClarty (2007): self-defeating behaviour
studies.finding: Low self-esteem people may think and act in self-defeating ways that diminish their quality of life.

studies.title: Kalpidou et al. (2011); Mehdizadeh (2010); Vogel et al. (2014): social networking
studies.finding: Students with lower self-esteem spent more time on Facebook and other social networking sites.

studies.title: Bushman, Moeller & Crocker (2011): valuing self-esteem boosts
studies.finding: Students valued self-esteem boosts such as praise or high grades more than favourite food, alcohol, friends, a paycheck or sex.

studies.title: Van Hiel & Brebels (2011): politics
studies.finding: Among older people (average age 71) in Belgium and the US, conservative beliefs were linked to high self-esteem.

studies.title: Ziegler-Hill & Myers (2009): voting
studies.finding: In the 2008 US primaries and election, people preferred candidates they believed had higher self-esteem.

studies.title: Gentile, Twenge & Campbell (2010); Orth et al.: life-span changes
studies.finding: Self-esteem rises through adolescence and adulthood, peaks around age 60 and then declines.

studies.title: Huang (2010b): Taiwan
studies.finding: In Taiwan self-esteem rose through childhood, adolescence and early adulthood but changed little after 30.

studies.title: Wagner, Lang, Neyer & Wagner (2014): Germany
studies.finding: Being married and high subjective well-being were linked to high self-esteem.

studies.title: Shaw, Liang & Krause (2010): Black and White self-esteem
studies.finding: Black teenagers reported higher self-esteem than White teenagers; Black self-esteem rose through adulthood but fell more steeply after 60.

studies.title: Eaton, Livingston & McAdoo (2010); Peteet et al. (2014): Black students
studies.finding: Black women students strongly identifying with Black culture had higher self-esteem; Black students feeling incompetent despite contrary evidence had high stress and low self-esteem.

studies.title: Schmitt & Allik (2005) and others: 50+ countries
studies.finding: Japanese college students consistently scored lowest in self-esteem.

studies.title: Fong & Mashek (2014): Asian-American students
studies.finding: Asian Americans reported lower self-esteem than European Americans, but those with more dorm social connections scored higher.

studies.title: Caldwell et al. (2006); Swenson & Prelow (2005): delinquency
studies.finding: High self-esteem correlated with delinquency among Mexican-American teenage boys.

studies.title: Kim, Hogge & Salvisberg (2014): acculturation pressure
studies.finding: First-generation Mexican immigrants feeling the most pressure to adopt American culture had lower self-esteem.

studies.title: Verkuyten (2009); Lopez (2008): ethnic identity
studies.finding: Turkish and Moroccan immigrants in the Netherlands and Puerto Rican immigrants in the US with stronger ethnic identity had higher self-esteem.

studies.title: POI correlational research
studies.finding: High self-actualization scores related positively to emotional health, creativity, post-therapy well-being, academic achievement, autonomy and racial tolerance, and negatively to alcoholism, institutionalization, neuroticism, depression and hypochondriasis; in women 19-55 self-actualization developed gradually.

studies.title: Hoffman, Kaneshiro & Compton (2012): peak experiences
studies.finding: Americans aged 40-65 most often reported peak experiences of joy with others, achievement and personal growth.

studies.title: Ho, Chen & Hoffman (2012, 2013): cultural peak experiences
studies.finding: Mainland Chinese reported serenity; Hong Kong Chinese interpersonal joy and achievement; Brazilians and Portuguese developmental landmarks.

studies.title: Self-determination research (Deci, 2011; Podlog & Eklund, 2010; Sheldon et al., 2009; Stephan et al., 2010)
studies.finding: Among Australian footballers, Indian and Nigerian teens and older US women, the highest self-determination scorers improved most in behaviour and well-being.

studies.title: Chen et al. (2014); Church et al. (2013): ten countries
studies.finding: Research in ten countries supported self-determination's role in positive growth needs and self-actualization.

studies.title: Ferrand et al. (2014); Milyavskaya & Koestner (2011); Strizhitskaya & Davedyuk (2014): three basic needs
studies.finding: Satisfying competence, autonomy and relatedness in young and old people in the US, France and Russia was linked to high self-esteem, self-actualization and well-being.

examples.title: Dropping down the hierarchy
examples.text: A software engineer chasing a promotion (esteem) loses her job in a layoff. Suddenly rent and EMI payments (safety) are all she thinks about; the award she wanted no longer matters. This mirrors Maslow's recession example.

examples.title: Deficit vs growth need
examples.text: Skipping lunch before an exam creates a real crisis: you cannot focus until you eat (deficit need). Not getting to practise your guitar this week is disappointing but not a crisis; it can wait (growth need).

examples.title: A first-rate soup
examples.text: A home cook who perfects her fish curry with real originality may be more self-actualizing, in Maslow's sense, than someone producing mediocre poetry.

examples.title: Jonah complex at work
examples.text: A student is offered the chance to lead a college fest but declines, worried she will be exposed as not good enough, even though part of her is excited. The fear wins over the thrill.

examples.title: D-motivation vs metamotivation
examples.text: One person studies only to pass and get a job (filling a lack). Another, with a stable job, takes up astrophysics for fun and seeks harder problems (increasing tension to enrich life).

examples.title: Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation
examples.text: Coding an app because you love solving the puzzle is intrinsic; coding only because the client pays is extrinsic.

checks.q: Maslow's main objection to psychoanalysis and behaviourism was that they
options: ignored positive human qualities by focusing on disturbed or average people
relied too heavily on laboratory experiments with humans
overemphasized free will and conscious choice
placed too much stress on self-actualization
checks.explain: Maslow argued that studying only abnormal or disturbed people ignores happiness, contentment and peace of mind (p. 247).

checks.q: Maslow's 'fastest runner' analogy means that to understand human potential we should study
options: a random sample of average adults
the healthiest, most creative and mature people
checks.explain: To know how fast people can run you study the fastest runner, so he studied society's outstanding representatives (p. 247).

checks.q: Maslow's attempts to overcome feelings of ugliness through athletics illustrate Adler's concept of
checks.explain: The chapter calls him a living example of Adler's compensation for inferiority (p. 248).

checks.q: The event that led Maslow in 1941 to commit to a psychology of the highest human ideals was
options: watching a parade after the Pearl Harbor attack
checks.explain: A parade after Pearl Harbor changed his thinking (p. 250).

checks.q: Maslow called his innate needs 'instinctoid' because
options: they have a hereditary component, though the behaviours satisfying them are learned
they are identical to animal instincts and fixed in form
they are entirely learned in childhood
checks.explain: Instinctoid means having a hereditary component; satisfying behaviours are learned and vary (p. 250).

checks.q: According to Maslow, a person who loses their job in a recession is likely to
options: be driven again by safety and physiological needs
checks.explain: The order can change; job loss makes safety and physiological needs take priority again (p. 251).

checks.q: Maslow called the lower needs deficit needs because
options: failure to satisfy them produces a lack and a crisis
checks.explain: Failing to satisfy a lower need produces a crisis and a deficit (p. 251).

checks.q: According to Maslow, the self-actualization need first arises in
checks.explain: Physiological and safety needs appear in infancy, belongingness and esteem in adolescence, self-actualization in midlife (p. 251).

checks.q: Why do physiological needs play a minimal role for most people in affluent cultures?
options: A gratified need no longer motivates behaviour
They are learned rather than innate
They are weaker than esteem needs
They are replaced by cognitive needs
checks.explain: Once satisfied, a need ceases to direct behaviour, so these needs matter little in affluent societies (p. 252).

checks.q: Physiological needs have the greatest personal impact as motivators
options: in cultures where basic survival is an everyday concern
checks.explain: They matter most where survival remains a daily concern (p. 252).

checks.q: Maslow believed safety needs are especially important drives for
checks.explain: Safety needs are important for infants and neurotic adults (p. 252).

checks.q: Too much freedom and permissiveness for children is likely to
options: produce anxiety and insecurity by removing structure
checks.explain: Absence of structure threatens children's security and produces anxiety (p. 253).

checks.q: Which statement reflects Maslow's view of love and sex?
options: Sex is a physiological need but can be one way of expressing love
Love and sex are the same need
Love is a safety need expressed through sex
checks.explain: Maslow did not equate love with sex, though sex can express the love need (p. 253).

checks.q: Maslow suggested that failure to satisfy the need for love is
options: the main cause of the Jonah complex
a fundamental cause of emotional maladjustment
unimportant if esteem needs are met
checks.explain: He saw failure to satisfy love needs as a fundamental cause of maladjustment (p. 253).

checks.q: The two forms of esteem needs are esteem from
checks.explain: We need self-esteem (self-worth) and esteem from others (status, recognition) (p. 253).

checks.q: According to Maslow, lacking self-esteem leads people to feel
checks.explain: Without self-esteem we feel inferior, helpless and discouraged (p. 253).

checks.q: Maslow's remark that a first-rate soup is more creative than a second-rate painting means that
options: self-actualization is about fulfilling one's own potential in any field
checks.explain: Self-actualization is not limited to creative superstars (p. 253).

checks.q: A person who has met all other needs but is not self-actualizing will feel
checks.explain: Without self-actualization the person is restless and discontented (p. 253).

checks.q: Which is NOT one of Maslow's conditions for self-actualization?
options: Freedom from constraints of society and self
Not being distracted by lower needs
Having achieved fame or social status
Realistic knowledge of one's strengths and weaknesses
checks.explain: The listed conditions are freedom from constraints, no distraction by lower needs, secure self-image and relationships, and realistic self-knowledge (p. 254).

checks.q: Being secure in one's self-image and relationships, and able to love and be loved, is
options: one of the conditions for satisfying self-actualization
checks.explain: This is listed among the conditions for self-actualization (p. 254).

checks.q: A religious figure who takes a vow of poverty illustrates
options: satisfying self-actualization while frustrating lower needs
checks.explain: Such people satisfy the self-actualization need while frustrating lower needs (p. 254).

checks.q: The more common reversal of the hierarchy described by Maslow is
checks.explain: People may value esteem over love, believing love requires self-confidence first (p. 254).

checks.q: Which cognitive need is stronger?
checks.explain: The need to know is stronger and must be partly met first (p. 255).

checks.q: Maslow described bored patients who improved after taking on challenging activities as
options: intelligent people leading stupid lives in stupid jobs
checks.explain: This clinical evidence supported the cognitive needs (p. 255).

checks.q: D-motivation involves
options: striving for a specific goal object to make up a lack
checks.explain: D-motivation means striving to make up for a deficiency (p. 255).

checks.q: Metapathology results from
checks.explain: Failure to satisfy metaneeds produces metapathology (p. 256).

checks.q: Maslow estimated that self-actualizers make up
options: 1 percent or less of the population
checks.explain: He estimated 1 percent or less (p. 256).

checks.q: Which characteristic did Maslow describe as a requirement for self-actualization?
options: Dedication to a cause or vocation
checks.explain: Dedication to a cause or vocation is called a requirement (p. 256).

checks.q: One reason so few people self-actualize is that self-actualization is
options: the weakest need and easily inhibited
the strongest need and hard to control
a learned need few are taught
a need that appears in infancy
checks.explain: As the highest need it is the weakest and easily inhibited (p. 258).

checks.q: The Jonah complex refers to

practice.answer: Instinctoid is Maslow's term for the innate needs in his hierarchy. They have a hereditary component, so everyone is born with them, but the behaviours used to satisfy them are learned and therefore differ from person to person.

practice.q: What are the conditions necessary for satisfying the self-actualization need?
practice.answer: Maslow listed four: freedom from constraints imposed by society and by oneself; not being distracted by lower-order needs; security in one's self-image and relationships, with the ability to love and be loved; and a realistic knowledge of one's strengths and weaknesses, virtues and vices.

practice.q: At what age do the cognitive needs develop, and which is stronger?
practice.answer: The needs to know and to understand appear in late infancy and early childhood, expressed as natural curiosity. The need to know is stronger and must be at least partly satisfied before the need to understand can emerge. Both lie outside the five-need hierarchy.

The Jonah complex, named after the biblical prophet who fled his calling, is the fear that maximizing our potential will lead to situations we cannot cope with. We are both thrilled and frightened by our possibilities, but fear often wins, blocking self-actualization.

practice.q: What is the Personal Orientation Inventory?
practice.answer: The POI is a self-report test of self-actualization developed by Everett Shostrom, consisting of 150 pairs of statements from which the respondent picks the more applicable one. It is scored for 2 major scales, time competence (living in the present) and inner directedness (self-reliance), and 10 subscales.

D-motivation (deficiency) is striving for a specific goal object to make up a lack and reduce tension, as in seeking food when hungry; it applies to the four lower needs. B-motivation (metamotivation) belongs to self-actualizers: it seeks to increase tension and enrich life, moving toward states of being (metaneeds) rather than specific objects.

practice.q: What criticisms did humanistic psychologists such as Maslow make of behaviourism and psychoanalysis?
practice.answer:
Maslow, the founder and spiritual leader of humanistic psychology, objected to both of the dominant forces in psychology of his time, especially Freud's psychoanalysis.

His central criticism was that psychologists who study only abnormal or emotionally disturbed people ignore all the positive qualities of human beings, such as happiness, contentment and peace of mind. Building a picture of human nature from the sick, he argued, underestimates what people are capable of. Freud's theory was based on case histories of clinical patients and so, in Maslow's view, gave an incomplete and overly negative image.

Behaviourism also failed him. As a student he found a psychology course "bloodless" and unrelated to people, and although he was briefly enthusiastic about Watson's behaviourism, the birth of his first child convinced him that behaviourism could not capture the mystery of human life; he said anyone who had a baby could not be a behaviourist.

Maslow's alternative was to study the best examples of humanity, the most creative, healthy and mature people. Using his analogy, to know how fast people can run you study the fastest runner, not the average one. His theory therefore derives from research on fulfilled, self-sufficient adults and holds that we are all born with needs that drive growth. Thus humanistic psychology offered a positive, growth-centred alternative focused on health, potential and self-actualization.

practice.q: How did Maslow's childhood illustrate Adler's theory, and how did it influence the theory he developed?
practice.answer:
Maslow's childhood fits Adler's ideas closely. He felt ugly because of his large nose and inferior because of his thin build, and his parents mocked his looks; he described his teenage years as one big aching inferiority complex. He tried to compensate by forcing himself toward athletic achievement, a clear example of Adler's compensation for inferiority feelings. When sport failed, he turned to books and scholarship. His early memories of waiting outside the library and reading in an empty classroom show, in Adler's terms, the style of life he would build: a life of learning as the route out of poverty and loneliness. Later he met Adler, talked about him constantly, and borrowed his concept of social interest.

His childhood also shaped his theory. His mother was cold, cruel and favoured his siblings; he said his whole life-philosophy and research was rooted in revulsion against everything she stood for. His father was aloof and often absent. This lack of love and security is mirrored in his theory's emphasis on belongingness, love and esteem, and in his claim that sufficient love and security in childhood are prerequisites for self-actualization. His loneliness found relief in marriage to Bertha, which gave him belonging and direction, consistent with the importance he gave belongingness. Finally, his rejection of his mother's hostility fed his determination to show people capable of better than prejudice, hatred and aggression.

practice.q: Distinguish between deficiency (lower) needs and growth (higher) needs. Which type was Maslow more concerned with?
practice.answer:
Maslow divided his hierarchy into lower and higher needs.

Deficit or deficiency needs are the lower needs: physiological, safety, belongingness and love, and esteem (the chapter also notes D-motivation applies to these four). They are stronger and have greater priority, appear earlier in life (physiological and safety in infancy, belongingness and esteem in adolescence), are necessary for survival, and their frustration produces a crisis and a deficit in the person. They can be satisfied even in relatively poor external conditions.

Growth or being needs are the higher needs, above all self-actualization. They are weaker, appear later (self-actualization in midlife), are less necessary for survival and can be postponed without crisis. Yet satisfying them leads to improved health, happiness, contentment, fulfilment and longevity, and they involve realizing human potential. They require better social, economic and political circumstances, such as freedom of expression and opportunity.

In addition, needs need not be fully satisfied before the next emerges; Maslow proposed a declining percentage of satisfaction (85, 70, 50, 40 and 10 percent).

Maslow was more concerned with the growth needs, especially self-actualization. His whole method was to study the healthiest, most fulfilled people, and his work on metamotivation, metaneeds and characteristics of self-actualizers all deals with the growth end of the hierarchy.

practice.q: Describe the differences between the safety needs and the belongingness and love needs.
practice.answer:
Safety needs are needs for security, stability, order and freedom from fear and anxiety. They are the second level of the hierarchy and arise in infancy. Maslow saw them as important drives mainly for infants and neurotic adults. Children show them openly, reacting immediately to threats and preferring routine and an orderly, predictable world; too much permissiveness makes them anxious, so freedom must be limited and guided. Neurotic adults remain dominated by safety needs, avoiding new experiences and organising their world rigidly. In normal adults safety needs are mild, seen in saving, insurance and preferring a secure job.

Belongingness and love needs come next, once physiological and safety needs are reasonably satisfied, and arise in adolescence. They concern giving and receiving love and being accepted. They are satisfied through close relationships with a friend, lover or mate, through social groups and even social media. Maslow distinguished love from sex, which is physiological, though sex may express love. He saw failure to satisfy love needs as a fundamental cause of emotional maladjustment.

So the two differ in content (security versus affection and acceptance), timing (infancy versus adolescence), the groups most driven by them (infants and neurotics versus people whose basic and safety needs are met), and the means of satisfaction (structure and predictability versus relationships). Safety needs are also stronger, since lower needs are prepotent.

practice.q: Define metaneeds and metapathology with examples.
practice.answer:
Maslow proposed that self-actualizers are motivated differently from others. Instead of D-motivation, which aims to make up deficiencies and reduce tension, they show metamotivation (B-motivation), seeking to increase tension and enrich life. Since they are in a sense unmotivated in the usual way, Maslow proposed metaneeds toward which they evolve.

Metaneeds are states of growth or being rather than specific goal objects. Table 9.1 lists truth, goodness, beauty, unity or wholeness, dichotomy-transcendence, aliveness, uniqueness, perfection, necessity, completion, justice, order, simplicity, richness, effortlessness, playfulness, self-sufficiency and meaningfulness.

Metapathology is the thwarting of self-development that results from failure to satisfy metaneeds. It prevents self-actualizers from expressing and fulfilling their potential. They may feel helpless and depressed without knowing why or what goal would relieve them; the summary calls it a formless illness without a specific cause. Each metaneed has its own metapathology. For example, frustrated truth produces mistrust, cynicism and scepticism; frustrated beauty produces vulgarity and loss of taste; frustrated justice produces anger, lawlessness and selfishness; frustrated uniqueness produces loss of individuality and a sense of being anonymous; frustrated meaningfulness produces meaninglessness and despair; frustrated dichotomy-transcendence produces black-and-white thinking.

Critics later noted that Maslow's definitions of metaneeds and metapathology were inconsistent and ambiguous.

practice.q: How does Maslow's image of human nature differ from Freud's?
practice.answer:
Maslow built his image of human nature in deliberate contrast to approaches, especially Freud's, that drew on abnormal and disturbed people and so ignored positive human qualities.

Optimism. Maslow's view is humanistic and optimistic, focusing on health rather than illness, growth rather than stagnation, and virtues and potentials rather than weaknesses.

Free will. We have free will to choose how to satisfy our needs and actualize our potential; we are ultimately responsible for how far we develop.

Nature and nurture. Needs are innate but the behaviours that satisfy them are learned, so personality reflects heredity and environment together.

Uniqueness. Needs are universal, but their expression is learned and so unique; even self-actualizers do not behave identically.

Childhood. Early experiences can foster or inhibit growth, but we are not their victims; we have more potential to manage our lives than we realise.

Good and evil. Human nature is basically good, decent and kind. Maslow accepted that evil exists but saw wickedness as a product of an inappropriate environment, not inheritance.

Goal. The ultimate goal is self-actualization, the highest level of functioning, attainable under the right conditions.

Thus, compared with a theory built on sickness, Maslow emphasised health, choice, growth, innate goodness and the power to overcome childhood. (For details of Freud's own position, the earlier Freud chapter should be consulted.)

practice.q: What does correlational research reveal about self-actualization and personality characteristics?
practice.answer:
Much of this research uses Shostrom's Personal Orientation Inventory (POI), a self-report measure of self-actualization with two major scales, time competence and inner directedness.

Positive correlates. Higher POI self-actualization scores are positively related to emotional health, creativity, well-being following therapy, academic achievement, autonomy and racial tolerance.

Negative correlates. High self-actualization scores are negatively related to alcoholism, institutionalization for mental disturbance, neuroticism, depression and hypochondriasis.

These findings run in the directions predicted by Maslow's description of self-actualizers as emotionally healthy, creative, autonomous and accepting of others.

Development. POI research on women aged 19 to 55 supported Maslow's view that self-actualization develops gradually over the life span. Related studies (Taormina & Gao, 2013; Ivtzan et al., 2013) found people over 36 far more likely to self-actualize, consistent with his claim that the need emerges in midlife.

Peak experiences. Research on Americans aged 40 to 65 found peak experiences most often involved joy with others, achievement and personal growth, with cultural variation (serenity among mainland Chinese, interpersonal joy and achievement in Hong Kong, developmental landmarks in Brazil and Portugal).

Being correlational, these studies show associations but not causation, yet they lend general support to Maslow's portrait.

practice.q: Describe self-determination theory and identify its three needs.
practice.answer:
Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan) is described as a contemporary outgrowth of the essence of Maslow's self-actualization theory. It proposes that people have an innate tendency to express their interests, exercise and develop their capabilities and potentials, and overcome challenges.

Intrinsic motivation. Self-determination is facilitated by intrinsic motivation, doing an activity for its own interest and challenge, as opposed to extrinsic motivation, doing it for external rewards such as praise, promotion, pay or grades. Both intrinsic motivation and Maslow's self-actualization aim at fulfilling one's talents for inner satisfaction rather than external reward.

Three basic needs whose satisfaction leads to well-being:
1. Competence: feeling able to master difficult tasks.
2. Autonomy: freedom to base one's actions on one's own interests, needs and values.
3. Relatedness: feeling closely connected with other people.

Research. Studies of Australian footballers, Indian and Nigerian teenagers and older US women found that those highest in self-determination improved most in behaviour and well-being. Research in ten countries including the US, China, Peru and Japan supported its role in growth needs and self-actualization. Satisfying the three needs in young and old people in the US, France and Russia was linked to high self-esteem, self-actualization and psychological well-being.

practice.q: Describe Maslow's hierarchy of needs and the characteristics of needs. Do we always satisfy needs in a fixed order?
practice.answer:
Introduction

Abraham Maslow, founder of humanistic psychology, proposed that personality is driven by a hierarchy of five innate needs that activate and direct behaviour. He called them instinctoid: they have a hereditary component, though the behaviours used to satisfy them are learned and vary between people.

The five levels

1. Physiological needs, for food, water, air, sleep and sex, are the strongest. When unmet they override everything; a starving person craves only food. Once satisfied they no longer motivate, which is why they play a minimal role in affluent societies.

2. Safety needs, for security, stability, order and freedom from fear and anxiety, are most important for infants and neurotic adults. Children prefer routine and become anxious with too much freedom; neurotics organise their world rigidly; normal adults show these needs mildly by saving or buying insurance.

3. Belongingness and love needs involve giving and receiving love through friends, partners, groups and even social media. Love is not sex, and failure to satisfy love needs is a fundamental cause of maladjustment.

4. Esteem needs take two forms: self-esteem and esteem from others (status, recognition). Satisfaction brings confidence and productivity; frustration brings feelings of inferiority and helplessness.

5. Self-actualization, the highest need, is the fullest development of one's potentials. Without it a person feels restless even if other needs are met. It is open to anyone; a first-rate soup can be more creative than a second-rate painting.

Characteristics of needs

- The lower the need, the greater its strength and priority.
- Higher needs appear later: physiological and safety in infancy, belongingness and esteem in adolescence, self-actualization in midlife.
- Lower needs are deficit needs: failing to satisfy them creates a crisis. Higher needs are growth or being needs: they can be postponed, but satisfying them improves health, happiness and longevity.
- Higher needs require better social, economic and political conditions.
- A need need not be fully met before the next emerges; Maslow suggested declining satisfaction of about 85, 70, 50, 40 and 10 percent.
- Generally only one need dominates personality at a time, depending on which others are satisfied.

Is the order fixed?

Usually lower needs must be partly met first, but the order is not rigid. Circumstances can reverse it: a recession that costs someone a job makes safety and physiological needs dominant again. Some people satisfy higher needs while frustrating lower ones: people fasting to death for their beliefs, religious figures taking vows of poverty, and artists risking health for their work. A more common reversal is placing esteem above love, believing one can be loved only after feeling self-confident. Maslow also added cognitive needs to know and to understand, which lie outside the hierarchy but are essential for self-actualization.

Research support

Graham and Balloun (1973) supported the order of the five needs, and Tay and Diener (2011), studying over 40,000 people in 123 countries, found basic needs must be met before fulfilment. Disadvantaged youth focused on safety needs (Noltemeyer et al., 2012).

Conclusion

Maslow's hierarchy describes a general tendency for stronger, lower needs to take precedence over weaker, higher ones, culminating in self-actualization. It is not an unbreakable sequence: needs are partly satisfied, circumstances shift priorities, and some people pursue higher needs at the cost of lower ones.

practice.q: Describe the characteristics of self-actualizing people. What are peak experiences, and are they necessary for self-actualization?
practice.answer:
Introduction

Maslow based his personality theory on the study of emotionally healthy people. He estimated that self-actualizers make up 1 percent or less of the population, yet concluded that they share a distinctive set of characteristics (Table 9.2). Their motivation is metamotivation: growth from within toward metaneeds rather than striving to fill a deficiency.

Characteristics

1. Efficient perception of reality: they see the world and others clearly and objectively, free of prejudgments.

2. Acceptance of self, others and nature: they accept their strengths and weaknesses without guilt or distortion, and accept the weaknesses of others and society.

3. Spontaneity, simplicity and naturalness: they are open and direct, rarely hide feelings except to avoid hurting others, and are individualistic in ideas without necessarily being unconventional in behaviour.

4. Focus on problems outside themselves: they have a mission to which they devote their energy. Maslow called this dedication to a cause or vocation a requirement for self-actualization; through it they satisfy metaneeds and define their sense of self.

5. Detachment and need for privacy: they tolerate and even need solitude, depend on themselves for satisfaction, and may seem aloof though they do not intend to.

6. Freshness of appreciation: they experience sunsets, music or gifts with wonder each time and take little for granted.

7. Mystical or peak experiences: moments of intense ecstasy (discussed below).

8. Social interest: borrowing Adler's term, they feel empathy and kinship for all humanity and want to help, even when irritated by others.

9. Profound interpersonal relations: few but deep, lasting friendships with similar people; admirers' relationships with them tend to be one-sided.

10. Creativeness: inventive, original, flexible and willing to make mistakes, open and humble like unspoiled children.

11. Resistance to enculturation: autonomous and self-sufficient, governed by their own nature rather than social pressure, though not openly rebellious.

Table 9.2 also lists tolerance and acceptance of others, and the summary adds a democratic character structure.

Self-actualizers are not perfect: they can be rude or even ruthless and feel doubt, conflict and tension, but less often and less intensely than others.

Peak experiences

A peak experience is a moment of intense ecstasy similar to a deep religious or mystical experience, during which the self is transcended and the person feels supremely powerful, confident and decisive. It can occur in almost any activity. Research on Americans aged 40 to 65 found the most common peak experiences involved joy with other people, achievement and personal growth (Hoffman, Kaneshiro & Compton, 2012), while cross-cultural studies showed serenity in mainland China, interpersonal joy and achievement in Hong Kong, and developmental landmarks in Brazil and Portugal.

Are they necessary?

Peak experiences are one of the shared characteristics Maslow found in self-actualizers, so they are typical of them. However, the chapter explicitly names only dedication to a cause or vocation as a requirement, and notes that peak experiences can arise from almost any activity. A balanced answer is that peak experiences are characteristic of self-actualizers but the text does not present them as a strict precondition; critics also note that Maslow's definition of peak experiences was ambiguous.

Conclusion

Maslow's self-actualizers form an attractive portrait of psychological health. Critics argue it may reflect Maslow's personal ideals because his subjects were people he admired, but POI research linking self-actualization with emotional health, creativity and autonomy gives it some support.

practice.q: Why do so few people become self-actualizing? Discuss with reference to child-rearing practices and the Jonah complex.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Maslow saw self-actualization as an innate need that does not have to be learned. Yet he found that fewer than 1 percent of people achieve it; among college students only 1 in 3,000 qualified. The chapter offers several explanations.

1. The weakness of the need

The higher a need in the hierarchy, the weaker it is, and self-actualization, at the top, is the weakest of all and easily inhibited. It also emerges last, not until midlife. Because lower needs are prepotent, anything that frustrates them blocks self-actualization. Hostile or rejecting parents make it hard to satisfy love and esteem needs, so the self-actualization need may never emerge. Poor economic conditions keep people focused on physiological and safety needs. Moreover, higher needs require favourable social, economic and political conditions, such as freedom of expression and opportunity.

2. Unmet conditions

Self-actualization requires freedom from social and self-imposed constraints, freedom from distraction by lower needs, security in self-image and relationships, and realistic self-knowledge. Many people lack one or more of these.

3. Childhood and child-rearing

Inadequate education and improper child-rearing can thwart the drive in adulthood.
- Sex-role training: boys are typically taught to suppress tenderness and sentimentality, so that part of their nature never fully develops.
- Overprotection: children not allowed to try new behaviours, explore ideas or practise new skills become inhibited adults unable to express themselves fully.
- Excessive permissiveness: too much freedom produces anxiety and insecurity, undermining safety needs.
- The ideal is a balance of permissiveness and regulation.
- Sufficient love in childhood, and satisfaction of physiological and safety needs in the first two years, are prerequisites. Secure, confident children remain so as adults. This parallels Erikson's emphasis on early trust and Horney's emphasis on childhood security. Without parental love, security and esteem, self-actualization is difficult.

4. The Jonah complex

Named after the biblical Jonah, who was called to prophesy, feared the task, ran away and finally accepted his fate, the Jonah complex is the fear that maximizing our potential will lead to situations we cannot handle. We doubt our abilities; we are both thrilled and frightened by the possibilities, but too often fear wins.

5. Lack of courage

Self-actualization takes courage, effort, discipline and self-control. Fulfilment does not arrive automatically once lower needs are met. Many find it easier and safer to accept life as it is. Self-actualizers, by contrast, constantly test themselves by abandoning secure routines and familiar attitudes.

Supporting evidence

Research shows that people over 36 are far more likely to self-actualize and that the more basic needs are met, the more likely higher needs are satisfied (Taormina & Gao, 2013; Ivtzan et al., 2013), consistent with the importance of lower needs and age.

Conclusion

Few people self-actualize because the need is weak and fragile, depends on the satisfaction of lower needs and favourable conditions, can be stunted by unbalanced or loveless child-rearing, and is resisted by our own fear of greatness and reluctance to give up security. Yet Maslow remained optimistic: since we are not victims of childhood and have free will, the potential remains for anyone willing to take the risk.

practice.q: Discuss research findings on self-esteem: how people high and low in self-esteem differ, developmental changes, and cultural and ethnic differences.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Maslow's esteem need has two forms, self-esteem and esteem from others. He held that satisfied self-esteem brings confidence, competence and productivity, while its absence brings feelings of inferiority and helplessness. A large body of research supports and extends this view.

High self-esteem

People high in self-esteem have greater self-worth and confidence and feel more competent and productive. College job applicants with high self-esteem received more job offers and better recruiter ratings (Ellis & Taylor, 1983). They cope better with job loss (Shamir, 1986) and see themselves as higher in intellectual skills, agreeableness, morality and extraversion (Campbell, Rudich & Sedikides, 2002). In the US and Canada they were more likely to play school sports and showed less anxiety and defensiveness. Women with unstable self-esteem had a stronger desire to become famous (Noser & Zeigler-Hill, 2014).

Low self-esteem

Large-scale studies in the US, Iceland, Canada, China, Norway and New Zealand linked low self-esteem to anxiety, depression, smoking, dropping out of school, criminal convictions, financial and work problems, and strong reactions to negative outcomes. It is also linked to physical health problems and death anxiety, social adjustment difficulties (Crocker & Luhtanen, 2003), stronger feelings of rejection after exclusion (Nezlek et al., 1997), and self-defeating behaviour that diminishes quality of life (Swann et al., 2007). Students with low self-esteem spend more time on Facebook. Over a third of Canadian adolescents said their perceived attractiveness determined their self-esteem, and those more concerned about appearance had lower self-esteem. Failing at self-esteem goals brings anger, shame and worthlessness (Crocker & Park, 2004), and students value self-esteem boosts above food, money or sex.

Other behaviours

Among older adults in Belgium and the US, high self-esteem went with conservative political beliefs, and US voters preferred candidates who seemed high in self-esteem.

Developmental changes

The main text reports that self-esteem rises through adolescence and adulthood, peaks around age 60 and then declines (Gentile, Twenge & Campbell, 2010; Orth & Robins, 2014). In Taiwan it rose through early adulthood but changed little after 30 (Huang, 2010b). In Germany marriage and well-being were linked to high self-esteem. (The chapter summary gives a slightly different pattern: high in childhood, low in adolescence, rising in adulthood, falling in middle and old age.)

Cultural and ethnic differences

Black teenagers report higher self-esteem than White teenagers, though it declines more steeply after 60 (Shaw, Liang & Krause, 2010). Strong identification with Black culture raised self-esteem among Black women students, while feelings of incompetence lowered it. Across over 50 countries, Japanese students scored lowest. Asian Americans reported lower self-esteem than European Americans, but social connection in dorms raised it. High self-esteem correlated with delinquency among Mexican-American boys, and pressure to assimilate lowered Mexican immigrants' self-esteem. Turkish and Moroccan immigrants in the Netherlands and Puerto Rican immigrants in the US with stronger ethnic identity had higher self-esteem.

Conclusion

Research broadly supports Maslow's claim that satisfying the esteem need promotes competence and well-being while its frustration brings distress. It also shows that self-esteem shifts across the life span and is shaped by culture, ethnic identity and social connection.

practice.q: Critically evaluate Maslow's theory: on what grounds has it been criticized, how did he respond, and what has been its impact?
practice.answer:
Introduction

Maslow's needs-hierarchy theory is one of the best-known accounts of human motivation and the foundation of humanistic psychology. Its evaluation must weigh serious methodological criticism against considerable research support and broad influence.

Criticisms

1. Methods and data. Maslow did not use case studies, experiments or correlational methods, and admitted that by laboratory standards his work was not research at all. He called it pilot studies, said careful experiments would take too long, and believed he needed less data than other theorists because he was sure he was right.

2. Small, unrepresentative sample. His sample of self-actualizers, fewer than half interviewed in person, was too small to generalise to the population.

3. Vague procedures. He did not explain how he interpreted tests or analysed biographies, how he studied self-conscious subjects indirectly, or what made him classify particular people as self-actualizers.

4. Subjective selection. He chose people he admired by personal criteria that were not specified, and later admitted self-actualization was hard to describe. His list of characteristics came solely from his clinical interpretations and may reflect his own philosophy and moral values, describing his ideal person rather than an empirical type.

5. Ambiguous concepts. Metaneeds, metapathology, peak experiences and self-actualization were used inconsistently.

6. Innateness questioned. Critics ask why self-actualization must be innate rather than learned through a unique combination of childhood experiences.

The chapter notes that weak methodology is not unique to Maslow.

Maslow's response

He argued that although his theory lacked laboratory support, it succeeded in social, clinical and personal terms: it fitted most people's experience and gave them a structured way to make sense of their inner lives.

Research support

Later research gives partial support. Graham and Balloun (1973) supported the order of needs; Tay and Diener (2011) found across 123 countries that basic needs must be met before fulfilment; need satisfaction is related to lower neuroticism (Williams & Page, 1989; Lester, 1990). Belongingness research shows ostracism quickly harms self-esteem and affects memory. Self-esteem research links high self-esteem to competence and well-being. POI scores relate to emotional health, creativity and autonomy, and self-determination theory, a modern outgrowth, is supported across many cultures.

Impact

Partly because of Maslow's optimism and compassion, humanistic psychology became extremely popular in the 1960s and 1970s. Journals and organisations were founded and the APA created a division of humanistic psychology. Its concerns were reborn in positive psychology, whose leaders credit humanistic psychology as a forerunner. Maslow's ideas continue to influence personality, social, developmental and organisational psychology, and teachers, counsellors, business and government leaders and health professionals have found them useful.

Conclusion

Maslow's theory is scientifically weak in its original methods and vague in key concepts, and his portrait of self-actualizers may reflect his own values. Yet later research supports its central claims about the hierarchy and esteem, and its optimistic vision of human potential has had a reach beyond psychology that few theories can match.

summary: Maslow, founder of humanistic psychology, rejected psychoanalysis and behaviourism for neglecting positive human qualities and chose to study the healthiest, most fulfilled people.
His lonely, abusive childhood and inferiority feelings, compensated through athletics and scholarship, exemplify Adler's ideas and shaped his emphasis on love, esteem and security.
He moved from behaviourism to humanism after the birth of his first child, World War II and the influence of Benedict, Wertheimer, Adler and Horney.
Five instinctoid needs form a hierarchy: physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualization; needs are innate but satisfying behaviours are learned.

Lower needs are stronger and appear earlier; they are deficit needs. Higher needs are weaker growth or being needs that need better conditions; satisfaction declines up the hierarchy (85-70-50-40-10 percent).
The order can change (e.g., job loss) and some people pursue self-actualization while frustrating lower needs; a common reversal places esteem above love.
Self-actualization requires freedom from constraints, freedom from lower-need distraction, security in self and relationships, and realistic self-knowledge.
Cognitive needs to know (stronger) and to understand lie outside the hierarchy, appear in early childhood and are essential for self-actualization.
Self-actualizers show metamotivation (B-motivation), increasing tension to grow toward metaneeds; others show D-motivation; frustrated metaneeds cause metapathology.

Self-actualizers (1 percent or less) show efficient perception, acceptance, spontaneity, mission, privacy, fresh appreciation, peak experiences, social interest, deep relationships, creativeness and resistance to enculturation.

Few self-actualize because the need is weakest and easily blocked, because of poor child-rearing (sex-role training, overprotection, permissiveness, lack of love), the Jonah complex, and lack of courage.
Maslow's image of human nature is optimistic: free will, uniqueness, heredity plus environment, not victims of childhood, basically good, with self-actualization as the goal.
He assessed people through biographies, interviews, free association and projective tests; the POI (Shostrom) and Smartphone Basic Needs Scale are later measures.
Research supports the order of needs, the power of belongingness, the benefits of high self-esteem, cultural variation in self-esteem, and POI correlates of self-actualization.
Self-determination theory, a modern outgrowth, stresses intrinsic motivation and the needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness.
Criticisms target his small, subjectively chosen sample, vague methods and concepts; yet his theory was hugely influential and is a forerunner of positive psychology.
